events.title: States renew fight against Trump's mail-in voting rule
events.summary: A coalition of states is again seeking to block President Trump's sweeping Postal Service rule on mail-in voting, just days after the Supreme Court lifted a lower court's injunction against his executive order. The big picture: The Supreme Court's decision essentially said the states sued too early. Now, they're hoping the timing is right to kneecap the plan ahead of the midterms. The ruling didn't weigh the merits of Trump's order, which critics warn would expand federal power over state-run elections. Driving the news: The complaint , brought by 24 attorneys general and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, challenges the U.S. Postal Services' final rule outlining the implementation of Trump's mail-in voting provisions. The states argue that the rule "violates the Constitution and federal statutes many times over" and that they'll have to redesign ballot envelopes and build new systems to transmit voter lists to USPS with just weeks to comply. "If not stayed or preliminarily enjoined, the Rule will frustrate or outright prevent Plaintiff States from administering their mail voting programs in November and foreseeably disenfranchise voters who vote by mail," the complaint filed in Massachusetts reads. The other side: White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement that the Supreme Court's decision "was a major win for the security of American elections." "Radical Democrats continue to oppose commonsense measures that protect the security of mail-in ballots and ensure only Americans are electing American leaders," she added. Zoom out: Democrats and advocacy groups — joined by Madison, Wisconsin, and Travis County, Texas — also revived their challenges Tuesday ahead of the Postal Service's final rule's publication. A judge initially decided the Washington, D.C., lawsuit brought by Democrats was premature, finding — like the Supreme Court's majority — the challengers could not yet prove harm. But they now argue in their proposed complaint that USPS' final rule "will profoundly and unlawfully disrupt mail voting in every state. Catch up quick: The Supreme Court on Monday cleared a block on parts of the March executive order. The executive order calls for "State Citizenship List[s]" of eligible voters, and a proposed U.S. Postal Service rule says it won't transmit mail ballots for people not on a state list. An unsigned opinion found the states sued before suffering any injury. The government, the court said, would face "irreparable harm" if the lower court order continued to sideline Trump's plan. But it left the door open to future lawsuits. "If the Postal Service's final rule harms the States, they may challenge that rule" when the time comes, the opinion said. Zoom in: USPS' final rule, which landed on the Federal Register Wednesday, mandates specific ballot-envelope designs and says the Postal Service will generate state-specific mail-in voting participation lists. The Postal Service's rule said it would not implement the rule without relief from the injunctions. Friction point: The renewed challenge and ongoing litigation are playing out on a tight timeline, as several states are set to issue mail-in ballots in September, leaving little time to hammer out the proposed regulations. U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani of Massachusetts also issued a nationwide block on Trump's mail-in voting restrictions in August. It remains in place, but the administration has since asked for its removal, citing the Supreme Court's decision. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson warned in her Aug. 24 dissent that green-lighting the administration's order on the grounds that the states' challenge came too early "needlessly injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections." Go deeper: Trump's mail-in voting rules raise fears of federal overreach Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

events.title: The year tech started losing
events.summary: David’s view If you’re running for office right now, the future is a dangerous place to be. The backlash against hyperscale data centers has converted both Democrats and Republicans into AI skeptics, warning that the industry’s rise risks robbing communities of autonomy. The populist rage against Flock and its AI-powered license plate cameras, while smaller in scale, is a growing offshoot of this bipartisan rebellion. “We should be very wary of” any tech that promises to support “an ongoing database of the location of every American citizen.” said William Lawrence, the progressive Democratic nominee for a battleground House seat in mid-Michigan, whose anti-data center campaigning set the tone for other candidates. “This whole premise is profoundly un-American.” In San Francisco, a bipartisan team of attorneys general sued Meta for alleged “known harmful features” that, they argued, addict children to social media; Meta settled the case, promising new safety tools for children, after insisting that they had plenty of tools already. In Tennessee, Sen. Marsha Blackburn is running for governor on a promise to stop cell phone use in schools “from bell to bell” — one of the only ideas she shares with New York Gov. Kathy Hochul. It’s a marked shift from past campaigns where votes were courted with talk of the benefits of a high-tech future. Candidates once ran on rural broadband that they said could give every voter the same internet access that urbanites enjoyed, plus laptops on the desk of every public school student. That enthusiasm is missing in this year’s elections. The lack of a unified Democratic agenda, and the president’s usual reluctance to stay on message, has obscured the trend running under everything. Voters have grown more nervous about their futures and more nostalgic about what they’ve lost. “Even if you are living where your forefathers have lived for generations,” wrote the tech skeptic Paul Kingsnorth last year, “you can bet that the smartphone you gave your child will unmoor them more effectively than any bulldozer could.” Voters want to slow things down. Democrats and Republicans are offering them different ways of doing that. The Trump administration has taken joy in rolling back the renewable energy spending of the Biden administration, stopping wind and solar farms and pushing the auto industry back from its embrace of EVs and greater engine efficiency . Job growth is slower than it was under Biden; they sometimes describe that as cause for celebration, too. “After the deportations that we have seen during President Trump’s administration and the closing of the border… we don’t need to produce as many jobs,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent explained to CNBC last week. But more voters feel like they’re losing out, and that the industries driving growth right now have made their lives worse — to say nothing of their kids. Where is the techno-optimism? Not in any of the campaigns. The crypto industry has spent tens of millions of dollars to elect a “pro-crypto Congress,” but its ads don’t try to sell voters on the importance of crypto. And ads paid for by the prediction market and gambling industries don’t tout the virtues of those industries. They are, universally , about the issues that voters care about — or that pollsters say they care about. Because those pollsters also find that voters are queasy about the explosion of gambling, and don’t see themselves getting rich by holding onto the right digital coins. Most of the visible voter angst about change is about tech. But some of it is about the cultural change that people argue about, on their phones, with the other angry people that their algorithm has found for them. The recent elite-level Democratic debate about “Woke 1″ was premised on something real. Liberals were embarrassed about the ways they talked about race and gender in 2020, from the pronouns they plunked into their email signatures to the black squares they posted on Instagram. What they were really embarrassed about was their radical, temporary optimism about how that year’s crises would transform the country. The pandemic was going to convince people of the need for universal healthcare; the murder of George Floyd would tear down the carceral state; the end of the Trump administration would reopen the border for millions of asylum-seekers. Democrats now agree that they promised too much change, too quickly, and that Republicans benefited from the backlash. Anti-vaccine activists won the COVID wars; mass deportation advocates came back with more momentum than they’d had in 100 years. Democrats now talk about immigrants as “neighbors” who deserve to stay here, not as more aspiring Americans who should be let in to enrich and transform the country. This is just not a year to tout transformation. The electorate is looking for candidates who’ll protect what they have — jobs, homes, time — and not imperil it in the name of growth or progress. Room for Disagreement One massive exception to this anti-tech mood among Republicans: Industry stocks have surged since Trump took office. Any voter who owns them, individually or in an index fund, is doing better than he was before the new “golden age of America.” Notable In his The Midterms, Actually newsletter, Astead Herndon looked at why both parties were taken by surprise by the data center backlash. “People don’t want to feel like they’re guinea pigs in an experiment, and it’s not just Sam Altman who has contributed to that feeling. It’s also the politicians who have treated technological change as something they retroactively legislate after a crisis arrives.” For Politico, Gabby Miller and Owen Dahlkamp talked to AI industry insiders about the ways they’re responding to political rage. “Now some of Silicon Valley’s biggest dogs are entering the fight.” In his Slow Boring newsletter, Matthew Yglesias shared his own theories on why people aren’t happier about technological progress.

events.title: AI agents may raise conflict-of-interest risks, study finds
events.summary: Does agentic AI have a payola problem? A new Stanford research paper lays out a problem that is being largely ignored as AI takes over internet search and e-commerce: It’s becoming less clear whether recommendations by AI chatbots are driven by advertising dollars or genuine information. In the not-too-distant future, when you want a new toaster, you might just talk to an AI agent about it on your drive home from work, and the next day, your toaster arrives. Behind the scenes, five toaster companies might have bid on what the agent sees. How do you know you really got the best toaster, or the best price? Now extrapolate this problem to weightier areas, like healthcare or financial services and the consequences are pretty serious. If everyone has their own personalized AI agent that’s smart enough to navigate the consumer landscape without falling for misleading marketing, perhaps this becomes a non-issue. But what might be more likely is that the vast majority of people use free chatbots funded by ads. Government regulation might help, with laws that prohibit chatbots from providing advice without disclosing financial incentives. But it might be too opaque to properly police. The time to sort this out is now, before an adtech-like industry springs up around agentic commerce and it becomes too difficult to unravel. — Reed Albergotti

events.title: Stanley Druckenmiller's AI writing has split Wall Street down the middle
events.summary: Billionaire investor Stanley Druckenmiller. Bloomberg/Getty Images Stanley Druckenmiller's use of AI to write a viral op-ed this week has divided the financial world. The billionaire investor compared tools like ChatGPT to calculators or speechwriters. Some financial gurus said he should have disclosed his use of AI. Others said it's the new normal. When Stanley Druckenmiller speaks, markets listen. When the legendary trader uses AI to craft his message, investors can't stop talking. Druckenmiller has said he used AI to help write his viral op-ed in the Wall Street Journal this week. In the piece, he criticized Scott Bessent, the US Treasury chief and his former protégé, for ramping up bond buybacks in a bid to drive down Treasury yields. The billionaire investor — who worked with Bessent at George Soros' hedge fund and Fed Chair Kevin Warsh at Duquesne Family Office — told the Journal that he felt "kind of proud" at age 73 to be using AI tools like Claude and ChatGPT, which he compared to using a calculator or a speechwriter. Druckenmiller said he was much better at economics than writing, and defended the op-ed as representative of his views. "These are my ideas and I've been speaking about them for over 15 years, as anyone who knows me knows," he said. Paul Gigot, the Journal's editorial page editor, said in a statement to his own publication that "AI is a fact of modern life" and "nobody can doubt that his op-ed is his genuine opinion." Druckenmiller and The Wall Street Journal didn't immediately respond to requests for comment from Business Insider. Splitting the Street The market wizard's reveal has divided financial commentators on X. Some argued that he should have disclosed his use of AI, and that it detracted from the value of his latest message. Others said Druckenmiller's ideas are what count, and AI writing is the new normal . John Huber, the founder of Saber Capital Management, said in an X post that some people "view AI writing as a form of plagiarism" or "at least disingenuous." Huber added that, particularly in the case of an op-ed, if the "words aren't authentic, they lose at least some of their meaning and author risks losing credibility." 💯 Todd nails it here. AI can capture an author’s main points. But when the words aren’t authentic, they lose at least some of their meaning and author risks losing credibility. This is especially true if the piece is an op-ed https://t.co/h46kFb2wHP — John Huber (@JohnHuber72) August 25, 2026 Jason Calacanis, an entrepreneur and co-host of the "All-In" podcast, said on X that it was "unforgivable for a public figure to publish an AI-written piece without a clear disclosure in the first sentence." He followed that sentence with a facepalm emoji. "Undermines the entire premise of publishing a thought piece, because we can't tell what's yours and what's the magic black boxes' thoughts," he added. Chamath Palihapitiya, a venture capitalist and one of Calacanis' "All-In" co-hosts, dismissed the idea of an AI disclaimer as "virtue signaling." In another post, he wrote: "If Stan Druckenmiller isn't embarrassed to be a meat proxy , you shouldn't be either." Palihapitiya framed AI chatbots as superior to human writing, and said people shouldn't be precious about the latter approach. "It's like after matches was invented, still celebrating the arduous time to rub two sticks together," he said. "Dumb." Similarly, Joe Weisenthal, a co-host of the "Odd Lots" podcast, questioned X whether human-written copy will be viewed as superior to AI-generated copy in the future. "If one of the world's most successful investors and one of the world's most prestigious outlets have no issue with publishing LLM-generated text, I don't expect this to hold," he wrote. Cullen Roche, the founder of Discipline Funds, said on X that Druckenmiller's piece was consistent with his commentary for decades. He wrote: "Druck's been predicting a crisis in US government bonds for 40 damn years and people think AI created an inauthentic narrative here? :-)" Claudia Sahm, the economist who developed the recession indicator known as the " Sahm Rule ," celebrated Druckenmiller's decision not to "waste his time writing up why Bessent was wrong." She called his use of AI the "sickest burn of 2026." Jerry Muller, the author of "The Mind and the Market," poked fun at the discord around Druckenmiller embracing a new writing tool. "1950: leading investor ridiculed for analysis written with BIC ballpoint pen instead of fountain pen," he wrote . "Handwriting experts call foul." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Australia's social media ban for teens is going, uh, pretty badly
events.summary: Australia's social media ban hasn't stopped a lot of kids from using social media. Elena Medoks/Getty Images Australia banned kids under 16 from social media apps in December 2025. A new report shows that the ban hasn't been effective — plenty of kids are still on social media. Sneaky teens have found easy ways to evade the bans. Imagine for a moment that you're an Australian 14-year-old (if you  are  an Australian 14-year-old, well, thank you for reading Business Insider, first of all. You can skip ahead). Life is already hard enough — your toilets flush the other way, and there's that whole cane toad problem. But worst of all, as of December 2025, your government banned social media like Instagram, TikTok, and Snap for kids under 16. Crikey, right? But much like the resolve and perseverance of Olympic breakdancer ' Raygun,' you are going to keep forging your own path, haters and naysayers be damned. So you figure out a way (it's not hard!) to skirt around the age restriction and scroll, watch, chat, and post on your favorite social media apps. You, an imaginary Australian teen, are not alone. According to a report by parental-control tool company Qustodio, the Australian social media ban has been impressively ineffective. Bloomberg writes about the report: Some 26% of children between the ages of 13 and 15 were on TikTok as of last month, just one percentage point below the rate prior to Australia's groundbreaking rules coming into effect, the parental control software maker said. The rate for children between the ages of 10 and 12 is higher now than before the ban, according to the data. What Qustodio found across Instagram, TikTok, and Snapchat use, there was a distinct drop in use among 10-12 year olds and 13-15 year olds for a few weeks right when the ban started in December 2025. But after a few months, kids steadily got back on, nearing or matching pre-ban levels. Take a look at the TikTok user chart from November 2024 until July 2026. That blip in the middle is when the ban started — and now it's back up. The graphs for other apps looked similar. There was a dip in kids using TikTok right when the ban went into effect, but it's mostly recovered. Qustodio Qustodio's report is based on its own internal data of users — kids whose parents have installed its parental control and monitoring on their devices. They point out that their dataset focuses on kids whose parents already pay for their app blocking software, which means that the use of these social apps among across all Australian teens/kids is probably way higher. The general findings of this recent report are similar to what the Australian government's own  eSafety commission found  this spring: the amount of 10- to 15-year-olds using social media apps had only dropped from 86% to about 81%. Most teens surveyed said that they didn't find it difficult to evade the ban. That's partly because age verification is a tricky thing. For example, in the UK, some enterprising kids were drawing fake mustaches on themselves to get around age-restriction systems that used facial recognition. So where does that leave the teens? I'm not sure. In the months since Australia's ban went into effect, other countries have followed suit. Similar bans are either already in place or in the works in France, the UK, Indonesia, and Malaysia. New Zealand just proposed a similar law on Monday , although it hasn't been passed yet. It seems highly unlikely that, even if more countries impose these bans (or if the tech companies can figure out an effective method of age verification without huge privacy intrusions), we'll suddenly live in a world where young teens and kids aren't on any social media platforms. Sure, there might be some drop due to tighter barriers or simply because kids will be less interested in certain apps if their peers aren't using them. Social apps like Snapchat are probably no fun without friends, but something that's more about consuming content like YouTube will be just as compelling for kids. And although most adults agree that mainlining TikTok for 12 hours a day isn't good for most growing minds, there's plenty of room for debate about whether an outright ban on kids under 16 is the ideal way of balancing the potential risks and harms of social media (addictive algorithms, harmful content) with the benefits (connection with peers, self-expression). The settlement Meta agreed to on Wednesday might be a move toward a good middle ground here. It will create stricter time limits for users under 18: a 2-hour daily time limit that can only be lifted by parents, a "default block" from 12 a.m. to 6 a.m., and no push notifications during school hours. events.title: A former Democratic operative on what the party needs to keep from MAGA
events.summary: The News Not every book by a former “insider” is created equal. “ Nothing Left ” by Evan Barker is unusually rich and well-timed. Barker was a powerhouse fundraiser for the Democratic Party’s left, which meant she was in the room for crucial meetings between its biggest stars, before she got fed up with the movement and voted for President Donald Trump in 2024. Barker dished about her evolution on TikTok, in articles in The Free Press, and then in the book — which, she told me, she wished had come out even sooner. “The first three to four or five months after the election, I think there was a window of opportunity,” she said in an interview from her Bay Area home. “You had Gavin [Newsom] interviewing Steve Bannon and Charlie Kirk. They were willing to talk to the right. It just seemed like there was more openness about debating what needed to change.” When the second Trump administration grew less popular, she worried that the conversation had stopped. “Nothing Left” is a great look behind the curtain at how political fundraising really works, but it also has a thesis: That the “Democrats should take the best parts of MAGA and the best parts of Bernie and marry them,” Barker writes. This is a transcript of a conversation with Barker about the book, which has been lightly edited for length and clarity. The View From Evan Barker David Weigel: There’s a storyline on the left that it’s the 2016 Hillary Clinton campaign that is to blame for injecting identity politics into the party. Where was it actually coming from, the idea that the party should be more culturally progressive? From the center or the left? Evan Barker: They both do it! It’s this weapon that’s sitting in the room and one of them will pick it up and be like: I’m gonna whip out identity politics. There were hints of this with the Brent Welder campaign and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. In 2018, you’re working for Welder; he is a white male labor attorney in Kansas City, Kansas. The DCCC wants a Native American candidate who ends up winning. So, what was AOC’s first reaction to the idea of coming out there to campaign for Welder? At first she was amenable, but then there was this mob that formed online. I don’t really know if they were establishment types or what; I wasn’t paying that close of attention to Twitter at that time. But there was this meme of Sharice Davids, who’s now a congresswoman, next to Brent and Bernie, and I think AOC. And it was: Two white men attacked a woman of color. They were @ing AOC and yelling at her. And she wanted to pull out of the event. We got a phone call from her team, and they were just like: Yeah, we’re not sure if she’s gonna still do this. She doesn’t wanna be seen as somebody who’s not supporting a woman of color. Brent responded: No, no, no, it’s not about that. I have the best policies that will help women of color, so that’s why you should come out here and help me. I left this out of the book: Our final donor call was two hours before polls closed. Believe it or not, politicians call donors all the way up until the polls close on election day. She was, like, a max-out ask. And I remember her saying: “I agreed to this call, but I just researched your race. And I found out that you’re running against a woman of color. And I just think it’s terrible that you want to take her place. This is her turn.” That was foreshadowing for what would completely take over the progressive movement. You write that “AOC became a loyal lapdog for the establishment, while the establishment embraced the most divisive aspects of progressive rhetoric.” There’s a debate among centrists who don’t like that this happened; how much did this weaken the Democratic Party? How much did this weaken its institutions? The problem with the centrists is that they are socially to the left, but they’re economically to the right. And that’s just not a pairing that really attracts working class people. That’s not a good match at all. The progressives are socially to the left and economically to the left, which also I think can alienate working class people. The centrists like to just blame the progressives for all of this, but I think it’s unfair: They don’t acknowledge their own issues of not really delivering economic transformation for working class people. At least progressives will talk about those things, although the priorities shifted. I think the ideal faction would be anti-progressive and populist. That’s somebody that’s socially moderate to conservative, but economically left. I don’t think that faction really exists. I’m in that faction. Can you explain what the Race Class Narrative is? For example: “Grocery prices are really expensive right now, but we know that black and brown communities are struggling the most to pay for groceries. So we need to do X, Y, and Z policies to make groceries affordable for all people.” It’s identifying an economic issue and then racializing it, but then saying that you’re gonna do something that will help everybody. Is there anything Trump has done that you want the next president, even if they’re a Democrat, to continue? What do you like, that he’s done? The anti-DEI stuff, absolutely. I think it’s better for everybody if we don’t continue going down that road. Closing the border — obviously, I’m happy about that. Bernie Sanders even said he was happy about that. This might surprise you, but I support the philosophy behind the tariffs. I don’t like the way that they were executed by the administration. What are your thoughts about AOC as the standard bearer of the Bernie movement? Is she well equipped to do that? No, no. I don’t think that she’d be able to win the blue wall. I think she’s really talented, you know? She’s a good speaker. People on the right like to write her off as dumb. She’s not dumb. She’s very smart. But she doesn’t have that broad appeal because she is more focused on identity. And just based on what I know about her and my couple of interactions with her, I don’t think that she is actually going to run for president. I think that she’s too much like — she wants to get along. She wants her colleagues to like her. If Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer and Nancy Pelosi showed her polling that said she was not able to win and that it was gonna really hurt the Democratic Party if she ran, I don’t think she would run.

events.title: US seizes domains of Chinese botnet used to hack NASA, Justice Department, and the Senate
events.summary: The FBI has seized a series of domains that were used by a large-scale botnet to coordinate and launch China-backed cyberattacks against American targets. According to the Justice Department’s statement on Wednesday, the seizures of the botnet’s domains deny the operators access to the platforms. The botnet was allegedly used by the Chinese government to break into computers across the United States, including systems at hospitals, defense contractors, and several federal government departments. Prosecutors said the China state-sponsored group, known as QTFY, was run by a Chinese company called Nanjing Xinjiuwei Network Tech, which created and operated the botnet of thousands of compromised internet-connected devices. The botnet aimed to serve as obfuscation networks, which hide the malicious traffic of hackers to make their activity more difficult to detect. Per the Justice Department, QTFY offers computer hacking services to its customers, who include Chinese government hackers working for the Ministry of State Security, and allows them to use the botnet. The hacks date back to 2018 and affected NASA, the Federal Reserve, and the Departments of Energy, Justice, and Health and Human Services. The U.S. Senate was compromised as recently as 2026, according to the government’s affidavit seeking a court order to seize the botnet’s domains filed earlier this week. The Justice Department said that the domain seizures made the botnet and its command and control servers “inoperable,” as the domains were hardcoded into the botnet’s code and were critical for the botnet’s communication and essential operations. Network giant Lumen said in a blog post that it had observed the hackers profiling and targeting government agencies, the defense and aerospace sectors, and others for the past year, and shared threat intelligence with the FBI. events.title: ChatGPT expands its foothold in the nation's classrooms
events.summary: ChatGPT for Teachers is expanding for the new school year. Philipp von Ditfurth/picture alliance via Getty Images OpenAI is roughly doubling the footprint of its ChatGPT for Teachers product. The tool is a free version of the company's business plan, part of a bid to woo educators. More than 2 million US students now live in districts signed up for the product, OpenAI says. Teachers are heading back to school, and ChatGPT is coming with them. OpenAI announced 55 new partnerships with American school districts on Wednesday, roughly doubling the reach of its ChatGPT for Teachers product. The districts signed on represent more than 300,000 staffers and 2 million students. The product, a slightly tweaked version of OpenAI's traditional business offering, aims to bring teachers on board with AI tools and give districts oversight. The product is strictly for adults, since OpenAI is not yet integrating student accounts or student-facing features. Not everyone is on board with AI in the classroom, as more students use it to complete assignments. A Pew Research Center survey last year found that more than half of teenagers have used AI chatbots for help with schoolwork, and more still believe their peers have used them to cheat. Some parents have begun organizing against AI in schools . Leah Belsky, OpenAI's vice president of education, said in a press briefing about the ChatGPT for Teachers rollout that improvements in AI's capabilities make "teacher judgment, teacher guidance, and district oversight even more important than before." OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Teachers last November and has committed to keeping it free through June 2028. Districts in 30 states have now onboarded with the tool, OpenAI said, with the densest uptake in the Los Angeles area and in the Northeast. The company said several of the nation's largest school districts now participate, including Houston's. OpenAI's product includes onboarding and prompts tailored to educators. A company webpage suggests that teachers use ChatGPT to develop lesson plans and explanations on topics. OpenAI says it doesn't train its models for this product on information users submit to the chatbot. The company has also signed data privacy agreements that cover 16 states, it said. The company will provide its latest AI models to the product in "waves," Belsky said, adding, "The goal is really to keep teachers and districts at the frontier." She also said she hopes the product will help teachers "save time, support students, and strengthen their own professional judgment." Christine Mai, the Houston district's director of innovation, said on the briefing that her district has used ChatGPT to help staff write curricula and summarize documents. She said there has to be a "human in the loop." "The teacher is still the professional, right?" Mai said. "They still need to make the final judgment in terms of, if they're going to use AI in that way, then they are also responsible for making sure that it's accurate, that it actually will benefit the students." events.title: Capital F closes $17M debut fund with goal to back the future of the ‘female economy’
events.summary: Capital F , one of the few all-female-led VC firms, announced Wednesday the $17 million close of its debut fund. The firm backs companies building in the “female economy” — or the markets where women drive demand. That mainly falls into three buckets for the firm, Margaret Coblentz, the firm’s co-founder, told TechCrunch — women’s health, digital commerce, and AI tools. The latter is increasingly important since “women are disproportionately the victims of trust and safety violations,” Dawn Dobras, the co-founder of Capital F, added. Coblentz and Dobras spent the last 30 years running companies together. Dobras was notably the CEO of the clean beauty retailer Credo Beauty and spent a decade at Gap before moving on to the clothing retailer Charlotte Russe. Coblentz also worked at Charlotte Russe before launching her own luxury knitwear brand, which eventually exited. Coblentz said she and Dobras decided to come together and launch a firm after spending years at the executive top ranks and realizing that “there weren’t a lot of women there.” “If you had asked me maybe 15 years ago, ‘Are you going to go into venture?’ I don’t know that I would have said yes,” Coblentz said. She and Dobras started angel investing after their corporate careers and always knew that “who writes the check and who owns the company matters quite a bit.” They first worked together almost 17 years ago at Charlotte Russe and figured, well, second time was the charm. The result was Capital F, named after their favorite F words, Dobras said. “Things like future, fund, fantastic, and, you know, fill in the blank.” During the fundraising process, they hosted salon events across the country for the “VC curious” to bring more women into investing, and as a result, almost 80% of the fund’s LPs are women, including Jenny Ming, the CEO of Rothys and former head of Old Navy; Marta Benson, former CEO of Pottery Barn; and Linnea Roberts and her firm Gingerbread Capital. “We realized that many times women aren’t invited into the rooms to invest in funds,” Dobras said. Dobras said Capital F doesn’t back a founder until they’ve spoken to at least two of their LPs. “We’ve seen those relationships move into advisor, into board members, into additional investments,” she continued, “and most importantly, lots and lots of sales introductions.” The journey to raise this fund had its ups and downs. “We always say we’re going to write a book,” Dobras said. They were working with the disadvantage of essentially being new fund managers. “Really, the people who supported us and wrote those checks came out of those salons,” Dobras said. Over the past decade, there has been a lot of talk about the importance of investing in more technology that centers on women’s issues, such as women’s health, which has long been underfunded and underfocused. Coblentz said that, in many ways, those conversations have led to some innovations that are starting to have an impact. They also mentioned companies in their portfolio, like Malama, which offers doula support for people on Medicaid. The firm has cut checks to 13 companies. It backs early-stage companies, writing checks between $250,000 and $1 million. Portfolio companies include the telemedicine startup Hey Jane, the period-and-cycle-tracking platform Stardust, and Big Sur AI, which Google acquired last year. “That was a fun LP letter to write because we hadn’t even closed the fund and we’ve already had an exit,” Dobras said. They expect to finish deploying the fund by the end of 2027. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. events.title: 'Ironing board' seats to be replaced on Thameslink
events.summary: All 115 Thameslink trains will get new seat cushions and backrests, says Govia Thameslink Railway "Ironing board" seats on some commuter trains will get extra cushioning, the transport secretary has said, more than a decade after the government spent £1.6bn of public money building the fleet. Heidi Alexander announced that more than 60,000 seats on all 115 Thameslink trains would get new cushions and backrests, replacing much-criticised thin and hard seats. She said the work, set to begin in 2027 and last two years, was "public ownership of our railways in action" as part of the new Great British Railways programme. However, some have criticised how the Department for Transport (DfT) awarded a £1.6bn contract for the trains despite being warned of the seat discomfort at the time. The seat upgrades are part of wider improvements planned for the Thameslink network after Greater Thameslink Railway came into public ownership in May 2026 . Other measures included an increase in Gatwick Express services from December and a programme to refurbish train toilets and remove graffiti across the fleet. Alexander said: "We'll start getting rid of the dreaded 'ironing board seats' so passengers can enjoy comfier, more pleasant journeys on some of Britain's busiest commuter routes." She said wider rail reforms would continue under the planned Great British Railways organisation, which is intended to oversee rail services across England. The class-700 Thameslink trains were heralded by the DfT as "state-of-the-art" and "a fantastic deal" for taxpayers when they were rolled out between 2016 and 2019. That followed the DfT spending £1.6bn of taxpayers' money for German manufacturer Siemens to build the trains in 2013, following a bidding process which began in 2008. DfT's own procurement guidance document for the fleet, seen by the BBC, stressed that they should be "high capacity" and "reduced weight". It said the new electric fleet would have a design that "must cater for [about] 1,000 people to board or alight at one time" and a "2+2 seat layout to ease flow and provide standing space". Some have claimed that this aim to maximise capacity and standing space for commuters led to the seats being so thinly cushioned. Responding to Alexander's post on X praising the new re-cushioning project, Graeme Pickering, senior correspondent at Railway Magazine, wrote: "Might have been wise not to frame this as 'public ownership fixes private sector mess' when it was the DfT which procured said trains." Shadow Transport Secretary Richard Holden said "promises of improvement" on nationalised services were turning into "fewer trains, fewer seats, and more delays". Two years before the Thameslink trains were rolled out to the public, a prototype was unveiled at London's Excel centre in 2014. A panel of volunteer experts at Railfuture, the UK's leading independent rail passenger campaign group, went to have a look and was not impressed. In a report, they warned: "We found the seats very hard and imagine this will soon lead to complaints from passengers, particularly bearing in mind that some journeys on these trains will be up to 130 miles long such as Peterborough or Cambridge or Bedford to Gatwick & Brighton and taking over two hours." Passenger comfort was "severely compromised" and "we strongly urge reconsideration of the design before series production takes place", their report warned. Production went ahead without the seats being redesigned. The DfT argues that it was not possible to renegotiate a private sector contract until public ownership took effect earlier this year. The BBC understands more details will be released in the autumn on the contract negotiations for the new cushions. John Whitehurst, chief executive of GTR, said passenger feedback had played a key role in shaping the plans. "Our customers told us that comfort matters, which was why we'd been working on plans to improve seating on Thameslink services," he said. Thameslink operates services across the South East, including Sussex, Surrey and some areas of Kent. events.title: Exclusive: Waymo says there's no AI shortcut to self-driving
events.summary: Breakthroughs in AI are fueling hopes that more data and smarter models can provide a shortcut to self-driving vehicles. Waymo, after more than 15 years and 200 million driverless miles, says there is none. Why it matters: The answer could determine whether the AV race is a long, expensive slog that rewards Waymo's head start — or a new track that lets newer rivals hit the road faster. Driving the news: Srikanth Thirumalai, Waymo's vice president of onboard software, said in an exclusive interview with Axios that it takes more than just better AI to safely deploy AVs at scale. Waymo's goal from the start, he said, has been "demonstrably safe AI." But a growing reliance from competitors on single "end-to-end" AI systems introduces risks. "Even the best AI models with trillions of parameters still hallucinate... We don't have a choice to say, 'Let's hit refresh' ... There is no click reboot or reload or refresh [in] physical AI. You have to deal with the consequences of it." In a blog post published Wednesday, Thirumalai goes deeper on 10 AI lessons Waymo has gleaned from its first 200 million autonomous miles. Catch up quick: Waymo got its start as Google's self-driving car project in 2009, well before the modern deep-learning revolution. In the early days, it relied on many specialized models — one for pedestrian detection, another to tell when a light turns green, for example. Gradually it shifted toward fewer, larger foundation models, "riding the AI wave," Thirumalai said. Now companies like Tesla, Wayve and Waabi are going even further, developing AV 2.0 systems they say are capable of humanlike reasoning — "end-to-end" neural networks that process raw sensor data and directly output steering commands. Waymo says it has tried the same tools but concluded that there aren't enough safety guardrails. "What we found is that just pure end-to-end systems are not able to meet our safety bar at the scale that we operate," Thirumalai told Axios. Reality check: Thirumalai said Waymo published the blog post to counter a narrative that AI can provide a shortcut to safe self-driving, with public trust in the AV industry on the line. At the same time, it's a flex. The safety standards Waymo wants the industry to embrace — not to mention regulators and rulemakers — also play to its biggest competitive advantage: a big head start built on years of testing and real-world driving data. While it didn't name specific competitors, it laid out reasons why newer approaches to building AV systems could carry risks — effectively raising the bar those companies would have to clear. Zoom in: Waymo weighed in on one of the industry's biggest debates — whether cameras alone can solve full autonomy. When training its models, Waymo found that visibility was far better when cameras, lidar and radar worked together rather than when one or more sensors were eliminated. "The AI can only make sense of what it sees, and if you just can't see it, the AI can't do much," Thirumalai said. Between the lines: It's a direct jab at Tesla, which is betting on a camera-only, end-to-end autonomous driving system. Better AI can't fully compensate for inadequate sensing, Thirumalai said. He added the same is true for high-definition mapping, which some rivals say is unnecessary. The bottom line: Waymo spent more than 15 years building a commanding lead in robotaxis, and Thirumalai argued now that there is no "one silver bullet" to reaching safe autonomy. Waymo's experience as the industry leader gives its argument weight — but it doesn't settle the debate. Rapid advances in AI could still prove there's a faster path to autonomy.

On Wall Street , stocks made a subdued start to trading after a stronger-than-forecast inflation reading, while the dollar climbed. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 0.2%, as was the Nasdaq Composite , while the S&P 500 index was flat. The personal consumption expenditures price gauge rose 3.7% on-year in July, in line with June’s expansion, but topping the FXStreet-cited forecast of 3.6%. The core PCE index advanced 3.3% on-year in July, in line with June and the consensus. The core reading is the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge. ING Chief International Economist James Knightley said the inflation rate was a touch firmer than anticipated, but “that is OK”. “As long as the month-on-month rate continues to come in close to 0.2%, the annual rate of inflation will converge on 2% over time, but the question is how much more patience the Fed actually has. Markets continue to price a 25bp rate hike before year-end while economists, in general, still favour an extended pause for policy rates,” he noted. The pound traded at 1.3590 dollars on Wednesday afternoon, down from 1.3632 dollars at the equities close on Tuesday. Against the euro, sterling eased to 1.1664 euro from 1.1683 euro. The euro stood lower at 1.1651 dollars against 1.1671 dollars. Against the yen, the dollar was higher at 159.37 yen, compared to 159.25 yen. The yield on the US 10-year Treasury stretched to 4.66% on Wednesday from 4.65% on Tuesday. The yield on the US 30-year Treasury fell to 5.18% from 5.19%. Nvidia stood 1.1% lower ahead of Wednesday’s earnings, which will be released after the Wall Street close. Bank of America says the Santa Clara-based chip maker should deliver the “usual” 3% to 4% sales beat and raise but thinks what matters are balance sheet disclosures. “The beat is priced; the balance sheet is the debate,” Bank of America said, suggesting a “buyback pivot toward Apple-style payouts is the underappreciated 2H and CY27 catalyst to re-rate the stock”. Meta Platforms was also in the news, with shares up 2.3%, as it said it has agreed to pay US states as much as 18 billion dollars and to impose sweeping new limits on how teenagers use its social media platforms. The Menlo Park, California-based firm, which owns Facebook and Instagram, said the payment of 18 billion dollars can be used to fund youth online safety initiatives, among other state priorities. The payment will be distributed in annual instalments over a 10-year period. In European equities on Wednesday, the CAC 40 in Paris closed up 0.3%, while the DAX 40 in Frankfurt rose 0.1%. Back in London, falls in oil majors BP and Shell, and accountancy software provider Sage, limited progress. events.title: The London stock market dodged a bullet with Shein | Nils Pratley
events.summary: The London stock market dodged a bullet with Shein China’s fashion giant will list in Hong Kong with a shrunken price tag – and big questions over its business model In a parallel world, we might now be preparing for the arrival on the London stock market of Shein , the giant Chinese-founded fast-fashion retailer. Or it could have happened already. The possibility of a London flotation was a running story during 2024 and into last year as politicians from both main parties engaged in behind-the-scenes wooing. Shein was seen as a shot of tech adrenalin for a listless local listings scene, and an opportunity to advertise the UK’s openness to international capital. Instead, Shein will float next week in Hong Kong . To which one can only say: thank goodness for that. In a listings context, Shein was a cast-off. The company had rejected New York amid tensions between Washington and Beijing and hostile questions from US lawmakers over labour practices in its supply chains in China. London was merely the next-best option for a company whose owners seemed suspiciously anxious to find a stock market home in the west. London did its reputation no favours with its willingness to jump. The Financial Conduct Authority, in charge of listings, took the view that it was “not unusual” for UK-listed companies to carry legal risks around the world and that what mattered was disclosure to allow investors to form their own view. The Labour government sounded keen. Donald Tang, the banker hired as Shein’s chair, did a round of feelgood meetings . This positivity was punctured, however, in January last year when Shein’s general counsel in Europe appeared at the Commons business select committee and stone-walled. Did Shein source cotton from China, asked the committee chair, Liam Byrne. The company representative was not qualified to reveal such “detailed operational information”. Byrne had not even been asking at that point about allegations of use of cotton produced in the Xinjiang region, which has been linked to Uyghur forced labour. The company, it should be added, had already said it had signed statements of compliance to modern slavery acts in the US, UK and elsewhere. But Byrne’s view was entirely fair: “The reluctance to answer basic questions has frankly bordered on contempt of the committee.” The idea of listing in London soon went away – encouraged, it seemed, by pressure from Beijing. And so, Hong Kong it is. Note, though, how the company’s price tag has shrunk from the £50bn that was talked about during the London leg of the global tour. The valuation will be $27bn (£20bn). Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning That figure also reflects the other issue that has dogged Shein: political and societal resistance to the practice of shipping goods in small packages out of China to take advantage of tax breaks on low-value imported goods. The US has already closed such “de minimis” exceptions as part of President Trump’s tariffs wars; the EU says it will phase them out; the UK intends to get there by 2029 . Shein used to argue that its business model did not depend on tax breaks, but the reduced valuation suggests that investors do not regard the issue as irrelevant. In a world in which Shein had somehow managed to list in London last year, the valuation drop would have been felt here. The supposedly hot prize would look substantially less so. London dodged a bullet on this one. Those politicians who encouraged the flirtation might reflect that, while the stock market is obviously desperate for exciting newcomers, you’ve got to choose your targets carefully. Nobody is talking about a missed opportunity.

events.title: Trump’s new affordability push runs on highways, rail
events.summary: The Scoop The Trump administration is unveiling a new proposal aimed at turning the nation’s highway and rail lines into “multi-use” utility corridors that could hold critical infrastructure like transmission wires, fiber optic lines, and water pipelines. The plan, dubbed “America’s Great Corridors of Commerce,” is being billed by the Transportation Department as a “voluntary nationwide opportunity,” and comes as the administration looks for ways to drive down energy costs for Americans. The initiative, according to details shared first with Semafor, will allow state-level transportation agencies and railroads to lease out land alongside roads and tracks to private sector companies to develop new infrastructure. “America has always been at the bleeding edge of innovation. But we will lose the race to develop the technologies of the future if we cannot lower costs and get the government out of the way,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a statement. The new plan, he added, will “make energy more affordable and fuel American industry for generations to come.” The administration hopes that using existing “transportation land” will reduce the cost of projects while leveraging “categorical environmental exemptions to bypass lengthy reviews,” according to a release describing the proposal, which emphasizes the need to quickly build out these types of infrastructure. Know More The Trump administration is also billing the proposal as a way to better compete with China, arguing that the country is ahead of the US in building things like high-voltage transmission lines. One of the biggest obstacles to many new power transmission projects is opposition from local communities and zoning authorities, a problem that can be bypassed if new grid lines stick close to existing infrastructure. In recent months, the administration has ramped up its focus on things like artificial intelligence data centers for similar reasons. The data center debate has increasingly become a focus in the midterms as voters sour on the technology infrastructure. Republican candidates across the are trying to walk the line between appeasing anti-data center voters without straying too far from President Donald Trump’s push for building them. Notably, the new proposal follows the Trump administration’s cancellation of a number of major transmission initiatives. The Energy Department ended a $4.9 billion conditional loan commitment last year for a transmission project and scrapped three other transmission corridor proposals earlier this month. Trump’s focus on leveraging the land — which mirrors proposals that Biden administration officials , environmental groups, and congressional Democrats have advocated for years — offers an alternative to those prior cancelled projects by using highway and railroad-affiliated land. Alan Mitchell, a senior Manager for US federal policy at the Clean Air Task Force, a climate nonprofit, commended the Trump administration’s plan as a “step in the right direction” and a “serious, practical use of existing authority.” But Mitchell argued that the administration’s other actions — like the recent cancellations — could undercut the plan. “The administration needs to act consistently to get our country the transmission it needs where it needs it,” he told Semafor.

events.title: Meta agrees to sweeping changes to restrict kids’ access to its apps as part of settlement with states
events.summary: Under the terms of its $18 billion settlement to resolve claims brought by 29 U.S. states over children’s safety, Meta on Wednesday agreed to sweeping changes designed to restrict minors’ access to Instagram and Facebook. The changes include a daily time limit, a restrictive “Night Mode,” autoplay controls, and more. The social media giant says the new protections will automatically apply to users under 18 on Instagram and Facebook in participating U.S. states and territories, pending judicial approval. The majority of these controls are required to remain in place for 10 years. One of the most notable changes is that Meta plans to implement a daily two-hour time limit for teenagers on its platform. The limit can only be disabled with parental permission, and once the limit is reached, teens will be locked out of Facebook and Instagram. Meta says the limit will be cumulative across Facebook and Instagram, which means that time spent on both apps will count toward the two-hour total. The limit will also be applied if Meta detects someone is using multiple accounts. The company also said kids will be able to choose a non-algorithmic feed that isn’t personalized by its recommendation systems as their default. Currently, users have been able to temporarily see a chronological feed on Instagram and Facebook, but can’t set it as their default feed. Instead, the app pops up the algorithmic feeds each time you open the app. Now, parents and guardians can set their teenaged kids’ default experience to a non-personalized feed. Meta said it will also introduce a default “Night Mode” block on its apps between midnight and 6 a.m. that would prevent underage users from accessing, posting, or viewing any part of its platforms. A Meta spokesperson told TechCrunch that while the company already mutes notifications for teens at night, the new setting will block them altogether after midnight. Teenagers will also receive prompts after every 15 minutes of continuous usage on Facebook or Instagram. The new prompts will accompany the current prompts that teens see when their total daily usage hits 60 minutes. Meta will also block underage users from using extreme makeup filters, a move that expands upon its existing restrictions that prevent them from using cosmetic surgery filters. Additionally, the company will mute notifications by default during school timings, which it is setting as between 8 a.m. and 3 p.m. During those hours, teens won’t receive push notifications, except for DMs and alerts related to account security or safety. Another new setting will allow parents and teens to turn off autoplay. Meta says they will need to take a “deliberate action,” such as tapping or swiping, to see more content. Like and reaction counts on posts will also be hidden for underage users by default, whether the posts are theirs or someone else’s. While teens can already choose to hide like counts, now those counts will be hidden by default. Meta also said it’s strengthening its technology for identifying users who may be aged 13 to 17, even if they provide an adult birth date, to ensure they receive appropriate protections. The social media giant published an open letter asking TikTok and YouTube to join it in setting an industrywide commitment by also introducing a daily time limit, turning off access to apps at night, restricting notifications during school hours, and 15-minute usage prompts. Meta’s $18 billion settlement will be distributed to the states over 10 years, but 30% of the settlement, or about $5.3 billion, will only be paid if YouTube and TikTok implement the same limits. “All platforms should empower parents and support teens by putting the same measures in place, because we know that when teens are restricted on one app, they simply move to another,” the company wrote in a blog post . Meta said it will continue to prevent teens from following or interacting with accounts it considers age-inappropriate. It also will continue to default teens into private accounts and restrict suspicious adults from contacting them. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Radar makes podcasts searchable — and usable by AI agents
events.summary: Particle , the AI newsreader startup founded by former Twitter engineers, is shifting its focus to a potentially more lucrative idea: indexing the spoken conversations buried in podcasts and making them discoverable. On Wednesday, the company introduced Radar , a podcast search engine that not only transcribes podcast audio but also understands what it means, enabling it to pull out key quotes and highlights. The solution has business potential, as it’s already attracted interest from hedge funds looking for data that their agents can’t see, explains Particle co-founder and CEO Sara Beykpour. “Hedge funds have been the highest-volume customers that are directly integrating with the API,” Beykpour told TechCrunch. While journalists and researchers could also make use of the tools, other top-paying customers have included AI search platforms and data resellers. (The search API provider for AI agents, Exa , for instance, is among Radar’s partners.) The idea itself stemmed from one of the Particle news-reading app’s most beloved features. The app had used its API to source interesting podcast clips that it then included alongside related news stories in the app’s feed. Particle’s team realized the product’s value, but also that it was somewhat trapped in the news reader. As the movement around AI agents began to gain steam, the company decided to pivot and focus on building an API for its podcast intelligence product. “Our vision is really to have all new media intelligence and all audio intelligence in that API. One of the reasons why it’s an interesting space is that most API agents and services crawl the web and they’re focused on text. We are providing that layer with audio,” Beykpour said. “Agents are generally blind to audio; they can’t see it unless something or someone has transcribed it.” With Radar, the company transcribes more than 130,000 podcasts, making it the largest transcribed podcast service in existence. This includes all the Apple Top 200 podcasts across its 135 verticals, with 20,000 episodes added to Radar’s index daily. The podcast transcriptions include speaker labels and rich metadata, as Radar understands the entities — people, companies, brands, products, and topics — being discussed. It’s also able to track mentions of these entities across podcasts and send alerts whenever they come up, either when the mention occurs or as a daily or weekly digest. The alerts, which can be delivered via email, Slack, or webhook, can be customized with filters. These let users configure Radar to only send alerts when certain guests appear and discuss a particular topic, for instance. The search can also be narrowed in other ways, such as limiting it to top podcasts only. Radar can extract relevant self-contained clips, with timestamps, allowing users to both listen to and read the comments made. “We’ve pre-chosen notable clips, so if you can’t listen to the whole podcast and you don’t want to read a summary, this is the best way to just get an idea of what’s happening in that podcast,” Beykpour noted. Radar can also track the topics mentioned in the podcast, who or what was mentioned and when, listener ratings and reviews, the episode’s ads, and more. There’s even a dedicated podcast ads search engine that can find every episode where a given company advertises and track how it trends over time. This feature has additional monetization potential, alongside other tools offering political bias analysis, chart rankings data, audience size estimates, sponsorship data, and brand suitability. While all of this is available through Radar’s web interface, its real product is the API and MCP , which allows AI agents and other businesses to tap into this same intelligence programmatically. Radar is priced at $29 a month per seat, with a $399-per-month plan for businesses that includes 20 seats. API users have custom pricing, based on their needs. In the future, Radar plans to expand the service beyond podcasts to support other forms of audio, such as YouTube videos and news clips. events.title: 20pc more children are growing up in rental housing, as ownership rates plunge
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts More children are growing up in rental housing and moving every couple of years Children whose parents owned the home they lived in had far fewer moves as those who rented. ( ABC News: Curtis Rodda ) A new report by researchers at Adelaide University shows children who grow up in rental housing move every 2.3 years, on average. Around one-in-eight children who grow up in rentals have moved at least 10 times by age 14. The proportion of Australian children growing up in private rental housing jumped by 20 per cent between 2001 and 2023. More children are growing up in private rentals and facing housing insecurity, a new report finds, warning that it could have long-term implications for their development, physical health and mental wellbeing. The study by four researchers at Adelaide University — Amy Clair, Emma Baker, Lynne Giles and Claire Morey — has been released by the Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute today. By analysing a range of comprehensive and long-term datasets, such as the Household Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) survey and the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children, the authors attempted to determine the effects of Australia's multi-decade housing affordability crisis on children. The report found that as housing prices surged between 2001 and 2023, the proportion of households with children living in homes owned outright plunged 52 per cent. Those in social rentals fell 46 per cent as the public housing sector stagnated, those who owned with a mortgage increased 27 per cent and those in private rentals rose 20 per cent. Australia's true 'home ownership' rate is just over 50pc. Here's why How the census over-inflates the home ownership rate. Research lead and associate professor Amy Clair said the latter statistic was particularly concerning as children growing up in private rental properties moved every 2.3 years on average. "By age 14, a child in a private rental had moved an average of six times. By comparison, those in households that owned their home had moved a little over twice on average, and children in social housing had moved just over four times," she said. The data shows children growing up in households with a mortgage tend to have moved about three times by age 14, which is half as often as those in a family renting. However, those averages also mask more extreme housing instability in many cases. Around one in eight children growing up in private rentals had lived in 10 or more homes by age 14, compared to approximately one in 40 children living in a home owned with a mortgage, the research found. It may not surprise you to learn that few households with children were renting by choice, with only 7 per cent reporting they did so because they preferred it and 8 per cent saying they appreciated its flexibility, while more than half said they did not have a housing deposit saved and around half said they could not afford to buy. AHURI found the most common reasons for renting related to the lack of a deposit to buy a home and other affordability issues. ( Supplied: AHURI ) 'Housing a critical determinant of physical and mental health' The research also showed that children growing up in rental housing were more likely to live in a household suffering financial stress or poor living conditions. Roughly 18 per cent of households with children in private rentals were late on a housing payment, compared to about 7 per cent of households with a mortgage, while around 10 per cent of children in private rentals experienced overcrowding, which was more than twice the rate of children living in owner-occupied homes. Dr Clair said children's experiences were often ignored in the public discussion of housing affordability, partly through a lack of data about their housing status, and better information could help foster the housing conditions that allowed children to thrive. "However, Australia's data is fragmented, creating blind spots that hinder early intervention, response targeting and accountable policy." The report's authors surveyed a wide range of academic literature which generally found links between housing stability and improved developmental outcomes. ( ABC Radio Darwin: Kate O'Toole ) The report suggests that maternal and child health services, early childhood education, schools and primary care services could routinely collect indicators of affordability stress, overcrowding and dwelling problems, while population surveys could include indicators of thermal comfort, damp, mould, crowding, safety and amenity.

events.title: Ex-Meta scientists want to bring visual AI to the factory floor
events.summary: AI is transforming everything around us but, thus far, it has largely remained contained to the digital realm. Increasingly, however, startups are looking to take it into the real world. Perceptron , a startup started by two former Meta research scientists, is one such company. Founded in November 2024, the firm develops frontier vision models that aim to help machines more competently interact with their physical environments. This week, the company launched its latest model, Isaac 0.5, which its creators say is designed to provide machines with the ability to “perceive, reason and act” in industrial settings. Specifically, the software is capable of helping vision-guided robots navigate complex environments like warehouses or factory floors. It also helps companies extract visual intelligence from videos recorded by those bots. Isaac 0.5 is also being released as an open-weight model, so its parameters and training materials can be inspected by anyone. The startup was co-founded by Armen Aghajanyan and Akshat Shrivastava, who previously worked for Meta’s Fundamental AI Research (FAIR), the tech giant’s AI research division. The duo see their software as the future of industrial automated deployment. “Physical AI today forces a false choice: generalist foundation models that need multiple dedicated cloud GPUs for every instance, or narrow models that handle perception or control, but never both,” the company says. Aghajanyan and Shrivastava say their tool is unlike existing models in the space because it is general-purpose, meaning that it’s not built for one specific, repetitive task. Instead, they say, the model is designed to be flexible depending on the particular environment (or situation) it is in. In an interview, Shrivastava asked me to consider what goes into a simple physical process like organizing boxes: “Imagine there’s a robot being deployed to sort packages right now. What are the tasks it would need to do?” Such a relatively simple task indeed consists of many steps. A robot would first have to read the label on the package, do some spatial analysis to understand where the boxes are, and decide which one to pick up. If it’s picking up a series of boxes, it would have to plan which boxes to pick up and in which order. Perceptron’s software is designed to help robots find their way through each step of the process. To be clear, the industry already has software that can help machines do most of those tasks, but there are few programs that are designed to do it flexibly. Where does the data for this algorithmic alchemy come from? Models like Isaac 0.5 learn operational skills by ingesting gargantuan amounts of video training data. Perceptron says its new model was fed on a million hours of what is known as general video to teach its algorithm to identify particular settings, visuals, and scenarios. The company also relied heavily on what is known as ego video — video captured, typically through a GoPro or a wearable camera, from the perspective of a person completing a physical task — as well as UMI video , which are similarly used to teach AI systems movements by recording repetitive human actions. While Perceptron isn’t disclosing the sources of its training data, Shrivastava said that the company had “internally built petabyte-scale datasets that span across modalities, whether it’s images, text, video, etc. all the way through robotic trajectories.” The utility of a software that can help robots operate competently in warehouses is obviously vast, and Perceptron thinks it’s well-positioned to lead that wave of automation. The startup is ready to market its software to a variety of vendors, and thus potentially see its intelligence layer integrated into a broad array of industries. Those industries include manufacturing, logistics and warehousing, security, mobility, as well as media and entertainment. “Nothing like this really exists out there,” said Aghajanyan. “We’re really excited about it.” The company previously raised $16 million from Bessemer Venture Partners, The Explorer Fund and SmartGateVC in 2024, according to Pitchbook . TechCrunch understands the startup is in the process of closing an additional round. An earlier version of this story incorrectly reported recent funding details. events.title: Ring introduces a new encryption standard, makes it the default for cloud features
events.summary: Amazon’s smart home division, Ring, said on Wednesday that it is adopting a new encryption standard called TAKE (Throw Away the Key Encryption) as the default setting for video encryption and user control. The company says this standard lets it protect user privacy without relying on end-to-end encryption, which can restrict some features such as video search, video description, and shared trusted users. Ring says the standard involves using a rotating set of encryption keys that are temporarily stored in the cloud and can only be accessed by the company to power features that users may have active. Once the request is completed, the company will delete the keys within 24 hours. The standard also lets it temporarily decrypt and process users’ videos so it can offer cloud-based features like Smart Alerts, which can notify users when people, vehicles, or packages are in the camera’s field of view. “With TAKE, Ring delivers the intelligent features you love and rely on, like Smart Alerts, and then throws away and deletes the encryption key. Only you retain the keys to your video,” the company said in a blog post. Amazon’s white paper detailing the standard notes that it was developed with a base of Messaging Layer Security (MLS), an open messaging standard developed by the Internet Engineering Task Force. The company said that with TAKE, if you lose access to your device and buy a new one, you can authenticate yourself by standing near the Ring cameras to recover your encryption keys. Separately, you can use a passphrase, cloud-based backups, another approved device, or passkeys to recover your account. The company said that TAKE will be gradually rolled out to customers starting in September, and will be the default standard worldwide. Users can still manually choose end-to-end encryption instead of TAKE. Over the last few months, Ring has received a lot of criticism for its “Familiar Faces” feature, which uses facial recognition to identify visitors. events.title: Reform proposes £30 tax rebate for HMRC phone delays
events.summary: Robert Jenrick sets out policies aimed at helping small firms People on hold to HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) for more than 30 minutes would get £30 off their tax bill under a Reform UK government, Robert Jenrick has announced. Reform's economy spokesman said HMRC's treatment of taxpayers was "offensive to working people" and his party would tie the pay of senior HMRC officials to customer service targets. To prevent abuse, the tax credit for phone delays would be limited to two occasions in a given tax year, Jenrick said. HMRC said its customer service had "vastly" improved over the past two years, with average call waiting times now 11 minutes and more of its services being delivered online or through its app. In January 2025, the Public Accounts committee accused HMRC of seeking to "degrade its telephone service to drive taxpayers to digital channels" in a highly critical report. , external The MPs' report said nearly 44,000 customers were cut off without warning after being on hold for more than an hour in 2024 and "HMRC's treatment of taxpayers has damaged trust in the tax system". Jenrick highlighted the findings - which were rejected as "completely baseless" by the then boss of HMRC - at a media conference in central London. "Frankly, it is offensive to working people and I have had enough," said the former Tory MP. "So, we will give HMRC a big incentive to actually provide proper customer service. "I'm announcing today that under a Reform government, if you spend more than half an hour waiting for HMRC to answer your call, you will get a £30 credit off your tax bill. If HMRC delay, they can repay. "And to make sure that the staff actually hit their targets, we'll tie the pay of senior HMRC officials to their customer service performance." The HMRC said 80% of customer interactions now took place digitally, reducing the time spent on the phone to advisers, who were there to deal with vulnerable or digitally excluded customers or those with particularly complex problems. A spokesperson said: "Our customer service performance has improved significantly with average call wait times now around 11 minutes. "Overall customer satisfaction is at around 80% with more people than ever using our digital services, including millions using the HMRC app." Jenrick also pledged to scrap UK privacy rules in favour of a "light-touch" approach to data protection as part of a bid to slash "red tape" for businesses if Reform wins power. He said the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which mirrors EU legislation and was adopted as domestic law after Brexit, had "strangled" tech firms and small enterprises. The framework would be replaced by rules modelled on New Zealand's privacy legislation, which Reform says has the lightest-touch regime still recognised as being "adequate" by the EU. Labour accused Reform of wanting to "scrap vital safeguards that protect people's private data" with its "unworkable and unserious plans". events.title: Bill Gates wants to see a robot tax and ‘Human Reserved’ jobs to mitigate harms from AI
events.summary: Bill Gates posted a long essay to his Gates Notes site today, showing just how much the Microsoft co-founder has been thinking about the social impacts of AI. Gates is mostly in the Responsible AI camp, arguing that Pacing the Frontier , the open letter published by AI employees pushing for an AI slowdown, would be a good idea, but expressing skepticism that it would be sustainable. He also expressed excitement about AI’s benefits to science and healthcare, but worried about the labor impacts — all pretty familiar stuff if you follow Anthropic’s policy work . But there were a few genuinely new ideas that could change the conversation if they take off. For starters, he proposes a “robot tax”: Right now, if you’re an employer and you hire someone, you pay payroll taxes on their earnings. But if you buy a robot, you can usually write it off right away as a business expense. The tax system nudges you toward replacing people with machines. A tax would slow the rush away from human labor a little and raise money for retraining and a stronger safety net. He also proposes setting aside certain jobs as “Human Reserved,” essentially barring AI from being used in certain tasks. It’s an interesting idea, and one that would be easy for policy-makers to enact: We might set something aside as Human Reserved for economic reasons. For example, we may do it because allowing machines to take over a certain role will displace a large number of people who can’t easily change jobs. You can’t tell a 55-year-old who has worked in construction their whole career that they need to go work at an elder care facility and expect them to find it fulfilling. Sometimes the decision to make something Human Reserved will be driven by other factors. In health, for example, imagine a robot giving you the awful news that you have an incurable disease. There’s no technical reason why it couldn’t. Yet it shouldn’t. The Human Reserved domain will evolve over time — for example, we should consider setting aside some jobs now and phasing in AI slowly over years or decades with a commitment to preserve some jobs. We should also note that both ideas would put a pretty serious dent in the profits of the major labs, which may be why we haven’t heard much about them until now. In addition, there are still a lot of unanswered questions about who exactly would set these rules and what exactly the rules would say, if they were to be rolled out. Don’t miss out .
