events.title: Stanley Druckenmiller makes AI writing a billionaire flex
events.summary: Legendary investor Stanley Druckenmiller made AI writing seem like no big deal this week, telling NOTUS reporter Jeff Stein "of course" he used it to help draft a widely shared op-ed for the Wall Street Journal . Why it matters: The moment could mark a real cultural shift where AI writing is basically all good, at least among a certain set of influential elites. Where it stands: Among his intended audience in the financial world, Druckenmiller's article got more attention for its substance — a scathing critique of Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent — than for its style. The writing is infused with the telltale cadences of the AI-generated one-two punch — for example, "If the 30-year must trade at 5.5% to clear, that isn't a crisis. It is an invoice." Or this familiar construct: "This wasn't liquidity management, it was price management ... " State of play: Many folks on "fintwits," the finance community on X, formerly known as Twitter, not only seemed willing to overlook the method, but praised it: "Druck using AI to write the op ed is the sickest burn of 2026," Claudia Sahm, a former economist for the Federal Reserve posted . "Didn't even waste his time writing up why Bessent was wrong." The big picture: The WSJ's opinions section threw open the floodgates to more AI-generated op-eds in its response to the discourse. "AI is a fact of modern life. People will use it to assist in their work and writing, including with research, checking grammar, editing and more," WSJ opinion editor Paul Gigot said in a statement. "The question for us is whether what we publish from contributors reflects an author's original argument, and if the author has the standing and credibility to make it." "In Stan Druckenmiller's case, we have had a relationship with him for many years, and nobody can doubt that his op-ed is his genuine opinion." Worth noting: The WSJ newsroom, separate from Gigot's team, has a different policy on AI use. Friction point: The reaction was very different to the response earlier this month when Harvard professor Ricardo Hausmann was criticized for using AI to write a column for the Financial Times . The paper ultimately appended a note at the top: "It has come to our attention that AI was used to condense a longer draft of this column prior to submission to the FT and our own editorial involvement." "The FT editorial code of conduct specifically prohibits the use of AI in the writing process." Zoom in: Druckenmiller likened using AI to using a calculator. "There's a reason I moved from an English major to being an economics major," Druckenmiller told Stein. "I'm not embarrassed by it ... I write everything using AI now for the same reason I use a calculator when I do math problems." Between the lines: For the most part, plenty of billionaires already employ ghostwriters to spin up their op-eds, LinkedIn musings and social media posts. Transitioning to AI seems like a natural progression. Zoom out: For everyone else, it's not clear yet if they can get away with this. Druckenmiller's AI-gate comes in the context of a broader backlash to the intersection of AI and content. YouTuber Hank Green faced backlash after viewers of a video last month accused him of using AI to write his script. He later shared an policy on how he'll use the tech going forward. "Where do you draw the line of what's immoral and what is moral?" content creator and marketing strategist Sam Ogborn told Axios. Madison Mills contributed reporting.

events.title: Trump's "election integrity" threat: Defunding state and local police
events.summary: State and cities nationwide are rebelling against the White House's push to withhold millions of dollars in police and anti-terrorism funding unless they impose new voting rules. Why it matters: President Trump's effort to impose election policies that he hasn't been able to get through Congress has now drawn two lawsuits from state and local governments that accuse the administration of threatening to defund the police unless Trump gets his way. "They are trying to defund public safety and counterterrorism," Harris County (Texas) Attorney Abbie Kamin told Axios. Harris County, which includes Houston, and the other jurisdictions stand to lose millions in public safety grants unless they impose the controversial voting rules Trump wants: a plan to transition to paper ballots, proof of citizenship verifications, mandatory hand-counted audits of 5% of all ballots, and more. (A separate part of Trump's "election integrity" push got a boost Monday when the Supreme Court lifted a block on his plan to use the Postal Service to help limit deliveries of mail-in ballots. The plan still faces legal challenges.) Zoom in: Harris County joined Columbus, Ohio, Nashville, Tenn., and El Paso County, Texas, last week in suing the Department of Homeland Security over the agency's effort to withhold grant money. State and local officials say DHS's demands for costly and unnecessary voting restrictions have put them at risk of losing money for anti-terrorism teams, equipment to counter drone and bomb attacks, protective gear and overtime pay, among other things. "We have dedicated public servants of again all political backgrounds that are involved in ensuring that elections are run securely and fairly," Kamin said. "But what's happening here is the threat to public safety funding and withholding counterterrorism dollars that local law enforcement relies on for partisan political purposes for one individual, and that is Donald Trump." The other side: In July, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin threatened to withhold federal funding from state governments, echoing Trump's claim that there were thousands of noncitizens on state voter rolls. "I obviously can't force the states" to work with the administration, Mullin said then. But "we are not going to spend taxpayer dollars reimbursing the states that are refusing to secure their elections." "We fully expected opposition to common-sense measures designed to protect election security and safeguard the integrity of American democracy," a FEMA spokesperson said in a statement. "Election security is national security, and protecting our critical infrastructure remains a top priority for the Trump administration." Zoom out: Besides the lawsuit filed last week, 25 Democrat-lead states filed suit earlier this summer contesting Trump's demands on election procedures. Some Republican-led jurisdictions have expressed a willingness to go along with at least some of the voting changes Trump wants, particularly the use of a federal database to check against voter rolls for citizenship. But for the most part, officials nationwide have said state and local laws already are sufficient to run elections, audit them and maintain voter rolls — work that's constitutionally tasked to state and local governments. "This type of ask ... feeds into this false narrative that our elections are not secure, and that if we do not do these things that the federal government is demanding that local elections are compromised," El Paso County attorney Christina Sanchez. "That is so far from the truth." Just transitioning to paper ballots alone would cost her county $3 million, Sanchez said. The big picture: Losing the public safety grants would have a huge impact on their jurisdictions, officials said in the lawsuit filed last week. In Texas, Harris and El Paso counties are planning to use the grant funds to buy equipment that can detect hazardous materials and chemicals, explosives and biological weapons. Nashville and Columbus' city governments said they've previously used such funds to buy machines that can detect explosives and purchase SWAT team gear. Between the lines: This isn't the first time Trump's administration has tried to withhold federal funding from governments that it views as non-compliant with its wishes. Trump has threatened to cut funding to state and local governments that have sanctuary immigration laws preventing local police from collaborating with ICE agents, for example. The administration's threats have failed when challenged in court before. "We've been prepared for this since the beginning of the Trump administration, that they're going to try and play games with cities like Columbus' funding," City Attorney Zach Klein told Axios. "This is the latest example of Trump coming in," he added "It's illegal and it's unconstitutional."

events.title: Queensland allowed to use coal, gas for data centres despite renewable push
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Prime Minister Anthony Albanese attended national cabinet today. ( ABC News: Nick Dole ) Queensland will be allowed to power its data centres using gas or coal. The federal government had previously demanded states use renewables as a standard. At the meeting of national cabinet, state and territory leaders also agreed to make citizenship a condition of holding a gun licence. Queensland will be allowed to go its own way using gas or coal to power data centres, despite Prime Minister Anthony Albanese previously demanding states use renewables. State and territory leaders met on Wednesday to settle national standards for data centre construction, but instead agreed to undertake further work. Queensland Premier Crisafulli had pushed for an energy-agnostic approach and told the ABC the carve out was a "good win" for his state, which owns much of its own electricity infrastructure. Premiers are heading into national cabinet divided over how Australia should meet the rapidly growing energy demands of AI data centres. "It shows because we own our assets, both our distribution and our generation, we are able to control a different mixture of energy right across the board, and that enables us to bring on new energy opportunities," he said. Premiers and chief ministers met with Mr Albanese in Sydney to discuss issues including AI, domestic violence, bird flu, fuel security and the embattled national gun buyback. Ahead of the meeting, federal Energy Minister Chris Bowen had insisted the Commonwealth would legislate over the top of states and territories that refused to adopt the renewables standard. Queensland argued the state-owned nature of its energy infrastructure put it in a position to maintain a technology-agnostic approach, meaning gas or coal could be used to power its data centres. The Northern Territory also opposed the renewables focus and has indicated it would use gas to power data centre projects. Following the meeting, Mr Albanese said both jurisdictions were in a "different position" to other states, as he justified the apparent backdown on renewables. Queensland Premier David Crisafulli had argued for a technology-neutral approach. ( ABC News: Nick Dole ) South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas rejected suggestions the prime minister had been rolled on the issue. "What you see emerging from national cabinet is a genuine desire to make sure we work through the issues associated with a rollout of data centres in Australia in a way that has a degree of uniformity," Mr Malinauskas told 7.30. "And I think today's discussion was very much an example of us all being aligned on the best way to do that." Mr Malinauskas said there was unity about the principle that data centres should add to the electricity grid without negatively impacting the national energy market. "What we agreed upon is that renewables will principally be the form of energy that will power data centres in the future in Australia," he said. A communique released after national cabinet said the standards would "ensure consistency and clarity for investors, while protecting Australia's economy, strengthening our sovereignty and securing benefits in line with our national interests". The meeting of national cabinet also agreed to make Australian citizenship a condition of holding a firearm licence. ( ABC News: Nick Dole ) The prime minister said the new standards, which would also include rules on water usage and community consultation, would be legislated early next year. "We have buy-in on Australia's first national AI laws," he said. Ongoing discussions are expected to include ensuring data centres do not raise power prices for households and other businesses. Mr Bowen has consistently argued renewables were the cheapest form of energy to ensure this did not happen. But Mr Crisafulli has rejected this and insisted his state would be able to keep power prices low even where other energy sources were used. "We believe that we can control our data sovereignty, protect the rights of local communities, and enable that energy mix even with those data centres on," he said. Citizenship a condition of holding gun licence The meeting of national cabinet also agreed to make Australian citizenship a condition of holding a firearm licence, though the prime minister indicated there would be some exceptions. Albanese to override Queensland on data centres Queensland's rejection of rules tying data centre construction to new renewables projects means the federal government will be forced to legislate to override the state.

events.title: Chinese hotpot chain Haidilao bets on takeaway, new brands, lower-tier reach for growth
events.summary: Takeaway emerges as Haidilao’s fastest-growing segment as it diversifies its formats, expands into lower-tier markets despite a soft economy China’s largest hotpot chain Haidilao International Holding has seen takeaway emerge as its fastest-growing segment, with demand for single-serving meals like rice-bowl sets surging, amid positive revenue and profit growth in the first half. Takeaway revenue for the Hong Kong-listed group reached 2.05 billion yuan (US$305 million) in the first six months, surging 121.2 per cent year on year. The segment accounted for 9.2 per cent of total revenue, up from 4.5 per cent a year earlier, according to its interim results released on Tuesday evening. “China’s restaurant industry is highly fragmented – chains hold roughly 20 per cent of the market versus around 40 per cent globally. That means a well-run chain like Haidilao can still gain share even in a soft macro environment,” said Ivan Su, director of equity research at Morningstar. Over the six-month period, the group posted total revenue of 22.34 billion yuan, up 7.9 per cent year on year. Net profit rose 0.5 per cent to 1.77 billion yuan. The Haidilao brand’s dine-in customers spent an average of 97 yuan, little changed from a year earlier.

events.title: Inside the backlash over the Jeffries-Kushner meeting
events.summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries ' long-standing tensions with his party's left flank resurfaced this week after news broke of his meeting with President Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner. Why it matters: Jeffries will have to make nice with the left next year if Democrats win back the House with only a narrow majority. Blowups like this are not helping. The Democratic leader defended the meeting in a video posted to social media on Monday, saying that Kushner "asked for a meeting, and I took it, to discuss the affordability crisis." Jeffries (D-N.Y.) suggested Kushner, whose dealings with Saudi Arabia have drawn scrutiny from Democratic congressional investigators, remains a top oversight target. "No one is going to get a pass," he said. "We're going to hold every single member of the Trump cartel accountable, beginning on day one." What they're saying: The meeting was "definitely a signal about the kind of Speaker Jeffries would be," said Joseph Geevarghese, executive director of the progressive group OurRevolution. The meeting "reinforces the worry from our base that Jeffries' instinct is to negotiate with the Trump power structure rather than draw lines and fight it," he said. Geevarghese and Justice Democrats spokesperson Usamah Andrabi both noted the meeting comes after Jeffries said on Meet the Press that Medicare for All, a central pillar of the left's platform, is "not legislation ... that I support." "Opposing Medicare for All and having secret meetings with Donald Trump's son-in-law sounds more like the leadership of the Republican Party than the fighters Democratic voters are demanding in Congress," Andrabi told Axios. Jeffries, a onetime co-sponsor of Medicare for All who dropped off the bill when he joined party leadership, said in a later radio interview that health care must "be a right available to every single American." The Democratic leader said there are "different paths" to achieve universal coverage. Those include Medicare for All, he said, but "other folks within the caucus ... think that there are other ways to get there." What we're hearing: House Democrats and Democratic congressional aides, speaking on the condition of anonymity to offer candid thoughts about their party's leader, questioned why Jeffries met with someone who has no official role in the administration. "Of all the people he could meet with, this strikes me as odd," said one lawmaker. "I just wouldn't think Kushner would be the main guy to do that. Strange." Lawmakers and aides also said Jeffries has not issued any private, Democratic caucus-wide explanation for the meeting. Between the lines: "They have a relationship," a senior House Democrat told Axios of Jeffries and Kushner, noting that they "worked on criminal justice" together during Trump's first term . The meeting was focused on potential areas of common ground between Kushner and the Democratic leader, according to the New York Times , which first reported it. The two discussed housing, immigration and affordability, with Kushner suggesting Jeffries meet with White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, according to a source familiar with the matter. Jeffries said in a CNN interview Tuesday morning: "The American people want us in Washington to solve problems. And I'm not simply here to make a point, but I'm also here to make a difference." The other side: "The media is trying to make this a big deal, but members are trying to enjoy the last week of August recess. Lots of CODELS and some are working," said the senior House Democrat. One progressive lawmaker told Axios of Jeffries: "People have the common sense that he's the only person who's going to run for Speaker and most of us like him personally." "We deal with him privately rather than publicly ... If everyone knows it's inevitable he's gonna be the Speaker, why would anyone go on record?" The bottom line: "It's less who you meet with than what you do with the meeting," said Adam Green, the co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee. "When Gavin Newsom meets with a right-winger, he concedes points -- while Elizabeth Warren gets Republicans to go along with housing bills and free hearing aids," he said. Green added: "Time will tell what Jeffries does with this."

events.title: Raised on AI
events.summary: When my oldest child was born, I immediately set up Gmail and Twitter accounts in her name. I broadly announced her birth online and proceeded to plaster her photo across all sorts of platforms. In short, I began creating her digital footprint long before she could stand on her own two feet.  Fast-forward a couple of years to when my second kid came, and I had essentially the opposite reaction. I wanted to make sure I preserved her privacy. I didn’t want her birthday to be a matter of public record or her face to feed the algorithms. In time, I would go back and scrub much of the early footprint I had created for my first child as well.  What happened? I watched the promise of the early internet give way to the reality of its potential for abuse. I myself was already fully in the throes of smartphone and social media obsession. My wife, a pediatric nurse, grew increasingly alarmed at the number of children admitted to her hospital struggling with the effects of things like body dysmorphia or cyberbullying as a result of interactions on social media. We became those parents. The ones whose kids carry flip phones and aren’t on TikTok.  We are not alone in this. A surprising—maybe troubling—number of people I know who work at big tech companies also keep their kids at arm’s distance from technology. They lock down their phones, if they have phones at all, and keep them off social media. Hell, even Mark Zuckerberg doesn’t publicly post his children’s faces on Facebook or Instagram.   If the desire to limit kids’ use of technology was once a subcurrent, it has become a raging flood. Jonathan Haidt’s best-selling 2024 book The Anxious Generation helped propel the issue into the mainstream (despite criticisms of his conclusions from some developmental psychologists). Last year, Australia became the first country to enact a social media ban for children under 16. Other nations, from Austria to Indonesia, have followed suit, announcing similar bans. The US Supreme Court recently upheld an age verification law in Texas, which acts as a de facto ban, and several states have flirted with their own measures. School districts all over the country are banning educational devices like iPads and Chromebooks in favor of actual books. Kids themselves seem to be embracing this tech skepticism too: The hottest gadget among the Gen Alpha set is a vintage Sony Walkman. We have to prepare our children to live in the actual world we have actually created, not the one we wish we had. Yet there is no hiding from technology. It permeates nearly everything, everywhere. And so we have to prepare our children to live in the actual world we have actually created, not the one we wish we had. How can we help kids survive and thrive in what we have wrought?  It’s a question that feels all the more urgent in the era of AI. To help answer it, we brought in the editors of Anyway —an utterly fantastic magazine for teens and tweens that is so good in large part because it meets them where they are. (If there is a teen in your life, I highly recommend it.) They helped us with the stories you’ll see in this issue, and they asked kids to share in their own words how they are feeling about AI and what’s to come. What those young people told Anyway was complex, fascinating, and, to an incredible extent, thoughtful and sophisticated.  Meanwhile, I’ve loosened the digital tether—just a bit. I still don’t post many photos of my kids online, and I remain abundantly concerned about the perils of social media and AI.  But when my older daughter started high school, we retired the flip phone in favor of an iPhone. And my younger one now sports an Apple Watch. These devices have opened up the world to them in all sorts of ways. They help forge new friendships, building relationships that move seamlessly between digital and physical spaces. They allow my kids to roam free—or at least more freely—beyond the known spaces of our neighborhood and across the city.  Along the way, they’re learning and testing boundaries, just the way they’re supposed to. I guess you could say I am too.

events.title: AI models flub these intelligence tests. Can you fare any better?
events.summary: Puzzles and games have been central to AI development since the very beginning. Just as we humans like to test our smarts with crosswords or logic puzzles, developers can test how far models have advanced with a gaming gauntlet. The term “machine learning” was popularized in a 1959 article by the IBM computer scientist Arthur Samuel about an algorithm that learned to play checkers. Chess and the Chinese board game Go are famous AI test beds too.  Judged purely on its puzzling skills, AI is improving a lot—and quickly. In late 2024, a team of scientists from Columbia University showed that even the best models could figure out only 18% of the infamous New York Times Connections puzzles; by early 2025, some models could solve them near perfectly every time.  But puzzles do more than just highlight the inexorable advance of AI capabilities. Seeing where models succeed and fail—and where we humans still beat them—can provide a useful window into the technology’s strengths and weaknesses. Despite advances, today’s models still fumble: Subtle changes in classic riddles often trip them up, and visual puzzles are a particular weak spot.  Here you’ll have the chance to test your wits on puzzles that have stumped models at one time or another. Some might be as tricky for you as they were for the AI; others are so simple that they’ll have you doubting whether AI is really intelligent at all. Each one highlights at least one way in which machine and human cognition differ. If you ace the test, you’ll have proved that you can out-puzzle an AI—at least for now.  Spatial Reasoning Let’s start with a domain where humans have a huge advantage: spatial reasoning. If you’ve ever taken an IQ test, you may have done a mental rotation problem. These puzzles ask you to determine whether different images represent the same objects from different angles. Though today’s language models typically have the ability to analyze visual inputs, they still fail abysmally at these puzzles. For all the talk of how world models can help AI understand physical environments, LLMs still don’t seem to be able to manipulate 3D objects the way spatial thinkers like architects and mechanical engineers can. Mental Rotation Instructions : Choose the answer that shows the object in the prompt, but from a different angle. In each case, there’s only one correct answer! Memory & Adaptability Frontier LLMs have extraordinary memories; they were exposed to a monstrous volume of facts during training and can recite many of them faithfully. That’s an asset for outcompeting humans at trivia, but it can also be a liability. When a puzzle closely resembles one a model saw during training, the model may whiz by key differences and respond with what it memorized.  This held true in a 2024 study in which researchers from Google and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign trained and tested models on slight variations of a classic type of puzzle called Knights and Knaves. In these problems, some characters always tell the truth and others always lie, and you have to figure out who’s who. The same principle may be at work in a test called SimpleBench. These questions resemble more complicated problems that models likely encountered in training. Humans spot the trick, but even top-tier models trip. Knights and Knaves Instructions : The only thing you need to know to solve these puzzles is that knights always tell the truth and knaves always lie. Determine who’s what on the basis of what each character says. SimpleBench Instructions : Read these SimpleBench problems carefully, and you should be able to figure out the answers in no time. Abstract & Visual Reasoning AI doesn’t just bungle visual problems in 3D—two dimensions can trip it up as well. That’s a major factor in how well models do on the most famous ­puzzle-based benchmark, ARC-AGI. These problems require you to infer abstract, general rules from a set of examples. Models do better on ARC puzzles when they receive each grid not as an image but as a string of numbers that encodes the color of each cell.  Research suggests that even when models answer ARC-AGI questions correctly, they often do so using byzantine and non-­generalizable rules, whereas humans draw on simple visual concepts. Despite these disadvantages, models have gotten quite good at ARC-AGI over the past year, but some puzzles—such as the one printed here—still stump them. ARC-AGI Instruction s: Study the three pairs of grids shown below to figure out the rule that dictates how the ones on the left transform into the ones on the right. Then get out your markers or colored pencils and fill in the fourth grid using that rule. (The solution is the same no matter which way the grids are oriented.) Intuition It’s not just AI models that fall into traps. We humans have our own cognitive foibles, many of which AI does not share. Psychologists have designed problem suites that invert the SimpleBench phenomenon: For these questions, humans often give knee-jerk answers, whereas models will respond deliberatively. Some of the problems exploit errors in the ways that we intuitively do math; others are phrased so as to suggest obvious answers that fall apart if the question is read carefully.  Lightning Round Instructions : Answer the questions below as quickly as you can. Increasing Complexity In some cases, whether an LLM can complete a puzzle is a matter of scale. One study from researchers at Apple found that LLMs can ace simple versions of the Tower of Hanoi problem, which involves moving a stack of disks one at a time without ever putting a larger disk atop a smaller one, and river-crossing puzzles, in which a group of people must traverse a river according to certain rules. But only up to a point: As the number of disks or people hits six and higher, the models began to falter. In another study, researchers at the University of Washington, Stanford University, and the Allen Institute for AI observed that LLMs struggle similarly with logic grid puzzles, which require deducing the attributes of a set of individuals from a list of clues. The Apple paper went viral, but commentators questioned whether the results reveal a unique limitation of LLM reasoning—or just that it’s normal to make errors as complexity piles up. The River Instructions : Using the scenario provided, plan the trips necessary to get everyone across the river.  Logic Grid Instructions : Using the list of clues, determine who lives in each house and what style of music each person enjoys. There is only one possible solution. You may find it helpful to fill out the grid below to keep track of your deductions. Grace Huckins is an AI reporter at MIT Technology Review . events.title: Four in 10 Americans believe UFOs are alien spacecraft, poll finds
events.summary: Americans are more likely to believe that UFOs have an earthly explanation than to think they are spaceships from another planet, according to new polling from Gallup. Forty-nine percent of US adults believe sightings of UFOs are tied back to human activity or natural phenomena — fewer than in 2019, when 60% said the same. But in that time, the percentage who believe at least some UFOs are alien spacecraft (37%) hasn’t risen much; more Americans have just become unsure. The Trump administration has been releasing Pentagon files on UFOs , which could be adding to that uncertainty. Most Americans are, at least, convinced that Washington is hiding something: Nearly eight in 10 believe the US government knows more about UFOs than it has told the public. — Morgan Chalfant

events.title: Lawyers see imminent decision in third-country deportation case
events.summary: Lawyers are bracing for a ruling from the First Circuit Court of Appeals that could reshape the Trump administration’s third-country deportation program, just as the administration pushes ahead with a new deal to send migrants to Liberia. The appeals court heard oral arguments in in May, and a decision is expected imminently, attorneys involved in the case told Semafor. They’re challenging the Department of Homeland Security’s practice of expelling migrants to countries other than their own without notice or a chance to contest the deportation. “The government is violating the law with every third-country [deportation] it conducts,” said Trina Realmuto, lead counsel for the plaintiffs at the National Immigration Litigation Alliance. She noted DHS has repeatedly removed people with court-ordered protections to third countries. A district judge ruled in February that the policy is unlawful , but that pause was later lifted by another court. Even if the appeals court rules in the plaintiffs’ favor, Realmuto expects the administration to appeal to the Supreme Court. “All of these illegal aliens received due process,” a DHS spokesperson said. “The Trump administration is utilizing all lawful options to carry out the largest deportation operation in history, just as President Trump promised.” — Adrian Elimian

events.title: London rollout of robotaxis delayed amid lack of guidance for firms to follow
events.summary: Uber and Wayve had said they would start trips ‘later this summer’ but launch now looks unlikely this year The rollout of robotaxis on the streets of London is unlikely to happen this year, as regulatory and technical hurdles push back the ambitious schedule set out by the UK government. Only weeks ago Uber and London-based Wayve were granted the first minicab licences in the capital to allow them to offer self-driving taxi rides to paying customers – but with a human safety driver in place, for now – and said they would start trips “later this summer” before a full public launch . In 2025, Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, accelerated the proposed timeline for commercial trials of fully driverless taxi services by a year, announcing that they would start in the spring of this year. However, progress has slowed in recent months and Transport for London (TfL) has still not published the guidance that companies wanting to offer services must follow to win its approval. Last month, Christina Calderato, TfL’s director of strategy, told the London assembly’s transport committee that the transit authority would not be in a position to start accepting applications “for some time”. She said: “I do not think we are in a rush to get [the guidelines] out. There is a huge amount of work going on behind the scenes.” Uber and Wayve have said that more than 100,000 Londoners were on their waiting list for self-driving taxis. They are racing against Google-owned Waymo and its Chinese equivalent, Baidu’s Apollo Go, to launch self-driving taxi services in London. Robotaxis are now available to hire in more than 20 cities across the US, China and the Middle East. Earlier this month Zagreb became the first European city to offer autonomous rides to the general public, through Uber, but the service still has a human driver for “onboard monitoring”. On Tuesday, Waymo announced that it plans to launch commercial operations in Munich, Germany, late next year. Ben Loewenstein, Waymo’s head of policy and government affairs for the UK and Europe, told the Financial Times that the company was currently “working through the safety approval process” with the transport department and was waiting on TfL’s guidance to gain consent. He added that Waymo was working towards launching a fully autonomous service “by the end of this year” but would not say whether the company would be able to offer paid rides to the general public in that timeframe. TfL has granted 15 private hire vehicle licences to Ford Mustang Mach-E vehicles equipped with Wayve’s artificial intelligence driving software, as well as surround cameras and radar. A TfL-licensed private hire driver will sit in the driver’s seat during trips to intervene if necessary, although the software is expected to control the car. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Uber and Wayve plan to launch small-scale commercial pilots with a driver behind the wheel soon. For its fully driverless launch Wayve plans to switch to a new Nissan Leaf vehicle that is still in production and is due to launch later this year. Alex Kendall, Wayve’s chief executive, said the company never claimed it would have a fully driverless operation this year. “I don’t want to put a timeline on it because we want to make sure we pass through [the regulatory process],” he told the FT. “This work is continuing at pace. London is a significant step up in complexity compared to Phoenix or San Francisco.” Baidu only began testing vehicles in London at the end of last month and has said it plans to launch public rides next year. Operating taxis without a driver requires approval via a new process, known as an automated passenger services permit, with the government’s Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency. So far, no vehicles have been approved by the DVSA.

events.title: Court decision boosts Democrats in midterm spending fight
events.summary: Democrats got some good news when the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that political parties and joint fundraising committees do not qualify for the candidate rate for political spending, which is lower than what outside groups have to pay. If the ruling stands — still a big ‘if’ — it would benefit Democrats. Democratic candidates are often outraising Republicans in key races, and those candidates would receive more efficient ad spending rates than political parties. Republicans will appeal to the Supreme Court; National Republican Senatorial Committee spokesperson Joanna Rodriguez said, “This is the first word, not the last.” But Democrats are celebrating the decision, which blunts some of the Supreme Court’s ruling earlier this year allowing more coordinated spending between parties and candidates. The Democratic House and Senate campaign arms said candidate-funded campaigns remain “a fundamental advantage in the midterms.” — Burgess Everett

events.title: Hobart council advances ban on full-home short stays
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Council plan to restrict Hobart short-stay accommodation to be sent off for final approval The planning amendment would block about 20,000 homes across Hobart from being wholly converted into short-stay accommodation. ( ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough ) Hobart City Council's planning committee has approved a plan to restrict the creation of new whole-home short-stay accommodation in the city's residential areas. The proposed planning amendment would block about 20,000 homes from being wholly converted into visitor accommodation, though it will not affect existing permits. The proposal will be sent to the Tasmanian Planning Commission, which will have the final say on whether it goes ahead. A plan to block Hobart property owners from converting their entire homes into short-stay accommodation has passed another milestone, with the local council voting to send the proposal off for final approval. Council revives bid to curb whole-home short-stays A fresh proposal from the Hobart City Council would block about 90 per cent of the city's homes from being wholly converted into short-stay accommodation. The proposal, which aims to restrict the creation of new short-stay accommodation in the city, was considered by the Hobart City Council (HCC) at its planning committee meeting on Wednesday. The tweak to planning rules would block about 20,000 homes from being wholly converted into visitor accommodation, such as Airbnb or Stayz. "The draft amendment delivers a clear net community benefit through improved housing outcomes while still allowing the visitor economy to be accommodated," council officers wrote. "The primary purpose of the proposed amendment is to limit the impact of new visitor accommodation use on the availability and affordability of housing for long-term residents in the city. "It was informed by extensive background analysis, including data on housing and rental markets, tourism trends, existing visitor accommodation supply and planning approvals." Council officers said the plan delivers a "clear net community benefit" by improving housing outcomes, while still accommodating the visitor economy. ( ABC News: Kate Nickels ) More than 50 submissions were made while the plan was out for public consultation across June and July, with 15 supporting the amendment while 41 were in opposition. The representations in support of the amendment focused largely on the impact that whole-home short stays have on the rental market, housing affordability, neighbourhood cohesion and the function of residential zoning. Those against the amendment highlighted the benefits short stays have on the city's economy and tourism, their role in providing accommodation for workers and families, private property rights, investment certainty and the impact on small business owners. The planning amendment will now be sent to the Tasmanian Planning Commission (TPC) for final approval, with the council anticipating a public hearing will be held. Short stay rental host says 'hosting is an economic lifeline' Merrydith Callegari, who has been a short-stay rental host in Hobart for more than 10 years, addressed the planning committee ahead of the vote. She was opposed to the amendment and called for an opportunity to work constructively with the council to develop a framework where short-term rental owners and the council could work together. "Short-term rentals are a vital part of Tasmania's accommodation requirements, hosting is an economic lifeline for many hosts and related industries, they fill gaps that hotels can't, they give visitors a home," Ms Callegari said. "I believe banning does not give the result you seek … we need to make building easier, to support landlords, not tear them down — after all, if renting is too hard, landlords will stop renting. Councillors divided on if move will help rental crisis Lord Mayor Anna Reynolds said cities all over the world were dealing with an increase in short-term rentals, while housing stock continued to fall short of demand. "It's got to the stage where it's having a very significant impact on our rental market," she said. "We are losing young people to other parts of Hobart because they can't get a rental here. "This is rental stock that's been basically turned into small hotels in our suburbs." Anna Reynolds says short-stay accommodation is having a "significant impact" on the city's rental market. ( ABC News: Luke Bowden ) Cr Reynolds said the amendment was a "good compromise" and still allowed for permits in the CBD, while also not removing any existing permits.

events.title: Sainsbury’s creates 10,000 work experience opportunities to tackle youth employment crisis
events.summary: Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in Andy Burnham commended Sainsbury’s for ‘stepping up’ while his government addresses youth employment crisis Get the free Morning Headlines email for news from our reporters across the world I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice Supermarket chain Sainsbury’s will provide around 10,000 work experience opportunities for young people in disadvantaged areas, the government announced, as part of efforts to address youth unemployment. Beginning in October, the retailer's scheme will feature workplace visits, career workshops and hands-on placements across England, Scotland and Wales designed to help more young people enter work. The project will focus on communities with high levels of free school meal eligibility and significant numbers of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) – which currently exceeds one million nationally. Andy Burnham commended Sainsbury’s for "stepping up" while his government works alongside employers to "close the gap between the classroom and the workplace". This follows plans unveiled last month by the prime minister for technical education options for 14-year-olds, placing them on an equal footing with conventional academic routes Mr Burnham said: “The youth unemployment crisis has been ignored for too long. This government is making it a top priority and bringing back hope. “Last month we announced a shake-up of the education system, with the launch of new prestigious technical educational routes. Now we’re bringing employers, schools and colleges together to close the gap between the classroom and the workplace. “It’s great to see Sainsbury’s stepping up with 10,000 opportunities to help young people build confidence, gain experience and get a foot in the door. “I encourage more businesses across the country to do the same. Access to opportunity and work experience shouldn’t depend on who you know, it should be within reach for every young person wherever they live – and that’s what I’m determined to deliver.” The new “modern work experience programme” by Sainsbury’s will offer younger students a combination of school-based learning and workplace experience while older participants will receive support with CV writing, interview skills, job applications and career planning. Sainsbury’s, one of the UK’s biggest employers with 140,000 staff, said a quarter of its workforce is aged under 25. Chief executive Simon Roberts said: “Like so many of us, I started my working life at 16 on the shop floor and know first-hand how much getting that first job really matters. Few things matter more to us at Sainsbury’s than helping young people get on that first rung on the career ladder.” The latest data, published in May, showed the number of young people aged 16-24 neither working nor learning surpassed one million – nearly one in seven – for the first time since 2013, reaching 1.01 million in the three months from January to March. Former Labour minister Alan Milburn, whose interim report in May warned the figure could rise to one in six by 2031, said: “For too long work experience has been treated as an afterthought. Yet six in 10 young people who are Neet have never had a job. “Employers say lack of experience is the single biggest barrier to hiring young people – and young people say exactly the same. It’s a vicious cycle and it’s holding Britain back. “Sainsbury’s is helping break that cycle, reaching the communities where young people face the biggest barriers. It’s exactly the kind of practical action employers can take now while we build the fuller response this problem demands.” British Retail Consortium chief executive Helen Dickinson said opportunities in retail – a first step on the career ladder for thousands – were being scaled up. She said: “Helping more young people be work ready and those who need help breaking out of the no-experience, no-job doom loop is critical to addressing the Neets crisis.” Schools are being encouraged to sign up from September. Sainsbury’s will also work with The Careers & Enterprise Company and other industry partners to test approaches which could later be expanded to more stores and communities. Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said: “Work experience is welcome but what young people tell me they really want is jobs. “No amount of training schemes can cover up the fact that Labour have destroyed job opportunities for young people with their jobs tax and extra red tape. “That’s put the brakes on businesses hiring young people – giving us the highest youth unemployment in over a decade.

events.title: Macquarie Group dumps KPMG from audit contract
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Topic: Business, Economics and Finance Macquarie released a statement on Wednesday citing the ongoing scrutiny of KPMG. ( Four Corners ) Macquarie Group has announced it will drop KPMG as an auditor, amid an ongoing scandal relating to its handling of confidential information. Macquarie announced on Wednesday afternoon that its board held concerns over the firm's auditing practices, amid ongoing scrutiny of KPMG . "The decision follows continued scrutiny of KPMG Australia's audit practice, including information exposed by the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Corporations and Financial Services," the statement said. "It also follows Macquarie's formal enquiries of KPMG to consider its capacity to deliver the audit, as well as the nature and impact of ongoing issues at KPMG Australia." Macquarie Group has announced KPMG will be dropped from an auditing contract amid ongoing scrutiny into the firm's auditing practice. ( Reuters: David Gray ) The board said it would instead recommend incumbent auditor PwC auditor at the company's annual general meeting. KPMG also released a statement acknowledging the decision. "While disappointed by the outcome, KPMG respects the decision taken by Macquarie," the statement read. KPMG chief executive John Sams said Macquarie's announcement was "a clear reminder that the consequences of our past failings are real". "Rebuilding trust will require sustained action, transparency and time. I am committed to leading this change with honesty, transparency and urgency," he said. Whistleblower raised concerns 'through the appropriate channels' KPMG has faced scrutiny over the alleged misuse of client data and misconduct after a whistleblower brought their complaints forward in 2024. Public documents released by the parliamentary committee, shared with the whistleblower's consent, detail the nature of the allegations, including claims the firm mishandled the whistleblower's initial complaints. The whistleblower told the committee said they attempted to address the issues with the KPMG partners, the head of audit, senior leadership and independent directors, before reaching out to KPMG International's whistleblower hotline and global leadership. They ultimately turned to ASIC and Senator Deborah O'Neill, which triggered the parliamentary inquiry. Among the more serious allegations were claims KPMG had stored confidential board papers and "used in the pursuit of major audit tenders," the statement read. The whistleblower told the committee these were not "minor employment matters" and further claimed in one instance partners offered access to clients internal audit papers along to with a Telstra-issued laptop. The next public hearing is slated for September 4, 2026, in Sydney. events.title: Report finds rock art damage more extensive than thought
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Burrup Peninsula rock art report finds more damage to Murujuga petroglyphs Rock art from between 17,000 and 50,000 years old at Murujuga National Park, which contains more than one million petroglyphs. ( ABC News: Kelsey Reid ) A new study has found pollutants from previous industrial activity have damaged a larger area of ancient rock art on the Burrup Peninsula than previously thought. The area is home to heavy industry, including a fertiliser plant and Woodside's North West Shelf gas project. The rock monitoring program has funding for a fourth year, but traditional owners want a longer commitment. Pollutants from industry have damaged a larger area of ancient rock art in Western Australia's north than previously thought, but current activity is not believed to be speeding up its deterioration. These are some of the findings from a major scientific study of the impacts of air emissions on engravings as old as 50,000 years on Murujuga, or the Burrup Peninsula, more than 1,500 kilometres from Perth. Now in its third year, the Rock Art Monitoring Report, which is compiled by members of the peninsula's five Aboriginal language groups and a team of more than 50 Curtin University scientists, doubled down on its past findings that the carvings closest to industrial projects had degraded at a faster rate. The Murujuga rock art petroglyphs are up to 50,000 years old. ( ABC News: Alistair Bates ) It also suggested that the damage — porosity suspected to be a result of historical emission levels — is more extensive than was once known. Porosity describes tiny holes in the rocks' surfaces, changing their structure. There are more than a million petroglyphs scattered across the rocky Pilbara peninsula and its surrounding archipelago, depicting animals, spiritual figures and stories sacred to traditional owners. Since the 1950s, Murujuga has doubled as one of WA's largest industrial precincts and export ports — home to a major fertiliser plant and Woodside's North West Shelf gas facilities. One of the world's largest urea plants, owned by the multinational Perdaman, is also slated to begin operating there next year. Lead scientist Ben Mullins said the report found the strongest evidence yet that sulfur dioxide emissions were having the "most significant effect" on the petroglyphs, largely caused by the burning of fuel. "Transport fuels, shipping fuels industry all have some level of sulfur in their fuel," he said. A petroglyph of a lizard at Deep Gorge (Nganjarli) on the Burrup Peninsula in Murujuga National Park. ( ABC News: Alistair Bates ) "There's a lot of evidence that that was a lot higher in the 70s and 80s, and even since 2010, shipping fuels have massively reduced sulfur levels and sulfur dioxide emissions." WA Environment Minister Matthew Swinbourn acknowledged the larger area of damage, but said he was satisfied it was not getting worse. In a summary of the document, the change was credited to a correction in the statistical significance applied to porosity levels. Matthew Swinbourn says the report is "very good science". ( ABC News: Kimberley Putland ) He defended its trustworthiness after a key statistician raised concerns about last year's report . "It remains very good science and the work that's undertaken by the entire Curtin team, as I say, is a credit to Western Australia," he said. The release coincided with federal Environment Minister Murray Watt's long-awaited first visit to the region since approving a 40-year extension of Woodside's North West Shelf and Murujuga's inscription on the UNESCO World Heritage List . Murray Watt was joined by Matthew Swinbourn, Ben Mullins, Kevin Michel, Dorinda Cox and Audrey Cosmos. ( ABC News: Kimberley Putland ) Mr Watt's decision to extend the life of Australia's biggest gas project until 2070 was mired by controversy, with critics claiming it would not adequately protect the rock art and would accelerate climate change. Mr Watt said his department would review the latest monitoring report and update the conditions of the North West Shelf approval if needed. Murujuga Aboriginal Corporation (MAC) deputy chair Audrey Cosmos said her people were "always going to be sad about industry". Murujuga Aboriginal Corporation's Belinda Churnside and Audrey Cosmos. ( ABC News: Kimberley Putland ) Ngarluma director on the MAC board Belinda Churnside called on the state government to honour its pledge to support the rock art monitoring project beyond its fourth and final year. A rock monitor perches up at Murujuga.

events.title: Amos Food plans Hong Kong listing to expand global sweets empire
events.summary: The confectionery firm’s Peelerz gummies have become a viral sensation on TikTok. Now, it aims to raise funds to expand its overseas presence Chinese confectionery giant Amos Food is seeking a listing in Hong Kong, as the firm looks to capitalise on the viral popularity of its sweets brands by ramping up investment in its overseas operations. Shenzhen-based Amos – known for its Peelerz peelable gummies and TastySounds music lollipops – has seen its sales soar over the past few years, especially in North America, where its sweets have become a sensation on the TikTok short video platform. “Hong Kong’s international capital market can help Amos reach a broader pool of global investors, particularly those familiar with cross-border consumer businesses and overseas growth strategies,” she added. “A successful listing could strengthen the company’s financing capacity and corporate-governance transparency, supporting its expansion in markets such as the United States while improving its distribution network and brand building.” Amos posted revenue of 2.78 billion yuan (US$410 million) in 2025, up 77 per cent from a year earlier, according to its listing application. Net profit more than tripled to 600 million yuan, from 198 million yuan in 2024 and 137 million yuan in 2023.

events.title: Bill Gates says we’ve passed AI’s danger thresholds. Now what?
events.summary: It’s a glorious day in Kirkland, Washington, an affluent Seattle suburb on the eastern shore of Lake Washington. The temperature is in the mid-80s, and the sky is incapable of being any more blue. The view from the Gates Ventures conference room overlooks the Carillon Point Marina, where a flotilla of expensive boats bob in the water, and across the lake to the Olympic Mountains that define the horizon. It’s gorgeous. And vaguely terrifying.  Because if the scene is placid, the messenger is not. Seated across from me at a conference room table, Bill Gates is rocking back and forth in his chair, totally animated. And the more he has to say—about the threats of terror or economic collapse or just losing control of our AI systems—the more agitated I find myself becoming, too.  The philanthropist and former Microsoft CEO says he has been growing increasingly alarmed by the rate of change at which AI technology is advancing, especially since guardrails are not keeping pace. In a new essay published today , Gates argues that we have passed the points where multiple potential dangers should have been checked. “We’ve crossed the threshold in terms of [AI’s] bio-capabilities, cyber-capabilities, psychosocial capabilities, job-market-destruction capabilities, and even the lack of control,” he said in an interview with MIT Technology Review about his new memo . “I’m just stunned at the lack of concern and discussion outside of the industry.” In an effort to wake the world up to what he sees as a rapidly growing societal disrupter, the 70-year-old tech titan has begun sounding the alarm as a “shrill voice,” both publicly with his new essay (the first of multiple he plans on the topic) and in meetings with the press, and privately in conversations with industry, government, and civil society leaders.  And while Gates is calling attention to a number of issues, his warnings about the bio-capabilities of the current frontier models are especially chilling. “Any model that can make novel molecules should be monitored,” he says. “I view bioterrorism risk, versus a natural pandemic, as about 50 times more scary, more likely than a natural pandemic risk.” In addition to the cautionary notes, he also advances some novel ideas for moving society forward. Among them are the concepts of human-reserved jobs, and taxes on robots and tokens. (A robot tax is a longtime notion of his.) The former would preserve some societally agreed-upon jobs for human beings, which he notes may vary from one nation to another. The latter is a tax that sets aside money earned from AI usage that replaces human work.  And to be sure, there is also a hint of optimism. Gates is bullish on the ways AI will continue to transform agriculture and health care and education, for example, or the ways in which it can help us navigate bureaucracy. And, he argues, eventually we do get to abundance. But first? Turbulence. And lots of it.  MIT Technology Review sat down with the billionaire philanthropist to talk about the road that lies ahead, its dangers, and how it could someday take us to a better place.  The following interview has been edited for length and to improve clarity and readability. Mat Honan / MIT Technology Review: Thanks for doing this. I don’t know if you had something you wanted to open with, or I can just jump in.  Bill Gates: You know, one good question I’ve had is: Why am I speaking out now? MIT Technology Review: Literally, my first question! Bill Gates: It’s really two things. One is that we’ve crossed the thresholds in terms of the bio-capabilities, cyber-capabilities, psychosocial capabilities, job-market-destruction capabilities, and even the lack of control; we’re seeing signs of difficulties there. And all these years, people have said, “Okay, when we get close to these thresholds, we’ll really figure out how to let only good people use it, or how to not let it do these things, and maybe that’s when we won’t let people copy models.” And I’m in a state of shock that we’ve crossed these thresholds.  So the fact that we’ve gotten past these is one reason, and the second is that I’m just stunned at the lack of concern and discussion outside of the industry. Within the industry, it’s complicated because the industry doesn’t like criticizing itself, or players like criticizing each other. Some companies are hiring fewer entry-level workers, which you’d have to call a pretty modest signal. But it’s going to happen, and not in any long time frame—because the things that hold people back in terms of capabilities and reliability, all those things are being solved. And so for a substantial part of the white-collar market, you have very low-cost substitution. And then you can have an opinion on how quickly robotics come along. We’re not there yet, but it is stunning the progress being made there—a little bit more in China than in the US, but somewhat in both. MIT Technology Review: You talked about all of this happening so much faster than the internet revolution did, than some of these previous technological revolutions did. What type of timescale are you talking about? You pointed to the thresholds that we’ve crossed. In your view, have we already passed some sort of tipping point where there’s going to be this inevitable change?  Bill Gates: The past definitely is very misleading on this, and a lot of people lean on that. “Hey, no previous technology resulted in a net jobs reduction,” and they’re right. And I’ve given that speech.  But with any credibility that I have, this time is different. When you can replace human cognition for an extremely high percentage of jobs across every industry in the same time frame at modest cost, relative to human labor costs, and your error rates … will probably be lower than human rates. The past is just very misleading. The current economic statistics are very misleading. “ If you’re worried about AI, going to a data center protest is not the most effective way to start the debate about how we minimize these bad things. “ Bill Gates And to the degree there’s any expression of concern at all, it’s like, “Hey, don’t build data centers.” Well, you can stop every data center in the United States and it won’t change any of the issues that I’m talking about. Data centers will be built globally. If you’re worried about AI, going to a data center protest is not the most effective way to start the debate about how we minimize these bad things. Just like yelling at an oil company executive is not the way to solve climate change.  MIT Technology Review: You talk about the benefits of AI in your essay as well as the costs. How are you thinking about balancing that message? And are you hoping people get a little worried when they read it? Bill Gates: They’d better! events.title: With no friends left to burn, Trump is running out of diplomatic ammunition | Rafael Behr
events.summary: With no friends left to burn, Trump is running out of diplomatic ammunition Everyone can see that the Iran war has been a strategic disaster for the US, while a failing president pretends he is winning N ow is the twilight of Donald Trump’s supremacy. The US is still the richest and most heavily armed nation on Earth. That status is secure. The current president, contemptuous of law and indulged in lawlessness by a supine Congress, enjoys even greater power than the constitution allows. With those advantages it takes a special talent for incompetence to look as thwarted and impotent as Trump does with more than two years of his second term still to run. History will record the war against Iran as a turning point in the fortunes of the current US administration and a grievous wound to national prestige. Pumped with hubris after the audacious military operation to kidnap Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro , Trump believed an equally brisk triumph was available in the Middle East. The Tehran regime would be decapitated. The country’s hydrocarbon resources would then be available for US exploitation. Six months later, Iran is controlled by a new generation of hardliners. Emboldened by resilience under US and Israeli bombardment, they demand financial concessions from Washington as the price for peace – reparations and a right to toll the strait of Hormuz. The war is not over, it has just turned cold. Trump believes Iran’s fragile economy is close to collapse. He threatens to push it over the brink with “D-day” sanctions . The metaphor of second world war amphibious assault is supposed to make yet another round of financial coercion succeed where past embargos have failed. It is true that ordinary Iranians are suffering terrible privations, but repression limits their capacity to translate discontent into demands for political change. By contrast, US consumers, aggrieved by the inflationary consequences of the war , and confused about its purpose , get to express their unhappiness in midterm elections in November. The calculation in Tehran is that American tolerance for economic pain is low enough that Trump will be forced to blink first. It is a reasonable assumption: the need to declare mission accomplished to a domestic audience – even on terms that amount to defeat by any objective measure – drives an impatient president’s actions more than long-term strategy. If sanctions fail, diplomatic climbdown is the only remaining move. The Pentagon couldn’t revert to the all-out military option even if Trump ordered it, because Operation Epic Fury burned too much of the national munitions stockpile . This is where an asymmetry of cost and capability comes into play. Iran can frighten ships out of the Gulf with a few mines. It can harry neighbouring states with drones knocked together for less than $50,000 and dispatched from mobile launchers that are hard to target. The Patriot interceptors that protect US forces and their allies in the region cost $4-5m apiece. (More than 1,500 Patriots are thought have been fired in the war so far , leaving fewer than 830 in the US inventory.) That depletion has global repercussions, most pressingly in Ukraine where top-end US interceptors are essential for shielding civilians from Russia’s most sophisticated ballistic missiles. Trump’s attitude to that conflict has evolved from craven pro-Kremlin partisanship and an assumption of inevitable Russian victory to grudging respect for Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s fortitude and ingenuity in proving that assumption wrong. But the shift is not stable. It depends on undertakings by Nato’s European members to cover the cost of arming Kyiv. If Trump had used normal diplomacy to cajole European democracies into financing the defence of their eastern flank , it would count as a foreign policy success – rebalancing the relationship to both sides’ benefit. But he did it with credulous admiration for Vladimir Putin and deranged demands for territory in Greenland. As a result, the European drive to autonomy looks less like burden-sharing and more like a hedge against American perfidy. It isn’t just Europe where US allies feel burned. Gulf states that found themselves on the frontline of Iranian retaliation in a war they didn’t start or want, expected a more reliable umbrella of protection. They feel unrewarded for their decades of service, hosting US military bases and functioning as proxies for American interests in the region. Last week Trump abruptly cut short a joint military exercise with South Korea – a loyal Asian partner to the US. A rational explanation, and the one preferred by Seoul, was that US forces were overstretched by their Middle Eastern entanglement. Trump framed it instead as an amicable gesture towards North Korean tyrant Kim Jong-un, whose regime he judged to be “unthreatening and respectful”.

events.title: 'This is crazy. This is insane': Bill Gates has changed his mind about AI and jobs
events.summary: The News Bill Gates says it’s time to hit the AI panic button. The technology has crossed dangerous thresholds in biology, cybersecurity, white-collar work, and human relationships, Gates said in an interview with Semafor. His warning is a striking shift from three years ago, when he wrote that the coming “bumpy” AI job disruption would lead to a “manageable” transition and that the technology would help people work efficiently. Now, he says it will wreak economic catastrophe, with “far fewer” jobs than exist today, thanks to the speed of AI’s advancements and what he calls a non-existent response from government and tech leaders. “I am in a state of shock that I’m sort of the first one saying, ‘This is crazy. This is insane,’” he said. “I’m just deafened by the silence.” In a blog post published Wednesday, Gates asks technology and political leaders to respond more urgently to threats from AI — namely to create new policies to protect workers and to tax companies based on their use of it. One of Gates’ fears about letting AI continue unchecked is that society will turn against it entirely, derailing its potential to improve humanity, particularly through advances in science and health. “What is the backlash going to be as these jobs go away?” he asked. “It’ll make the data center thing look like nothing.” It is his first of several planned essays, Gates told Semafor, including one featuring a deeper analysis of biological risks from AI. “I wrote a whole book about how to avoid the next pandemic,” Gates said. “The bioterrorism risk is 50 times the natural pandemic risk now.” Gates said that in private, some technologists agree with his current stance, including Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman. “Mustafa feels the same way today that he felt when he wrote the book,” Gates said, referring to Suleyman’s warning in published in 2023, which says society was unprepared for the sweeping changes AI is about to bring. “He’s very, very glad I’m writing the memo.” Other prominent leaders, such as Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis, have also sharpened their warnings. Hassabis recently proposed a federally overseen frontier-AI standards body modeled partly on FINRA, funded largely by industry, and empowered to test advanced models before release. He said the system could eventually be made mandatory and coordinate a slowdown among frontier labs if necessary. In 2023, Gates, along with Suleyman, Hassabis, and hundreds of other tech and policy leaders, signed a statement saying the risk of extinction from AI should be treated as a global priority alongside pandemics and nuclear war. Know More A common refrain from AI optimists — and from economists skeptical of Silicon Valley doomsaying — is that every technology revolution of the past causes labor disruptions, but ends up creating far more jobs than it destroys. Microsoft President Brad Smith made that case in June, writing that AI “will displace some jobs, even as it creates others” and that “when technology increases supply, human ambition often generates more demand.” The question is whether the AI transition will happen so much faster than previous technological revolutions, that it will disrupt society at a pace faster than governments can reckon with. Gates said it isn’t the speed of the revolution that worries him. It’s the breadth. “There isn’t a job that isn’t affected,” he said, predicting that, in the majority of occupations, humans will eventually be “vastly inferior to the AI doing the job.” In other words, even if adoption takes time, the effect will be so widespread that the aggregate impact will be enormous. “It’s different not because the speed is different, but the breadth is what makes it utterly, utterly a unique moment in evolutionary history,” Gates said. Research supports the breadth point more clearly than Gates’ prediction of net destruction. The IMF estimates AI could affect nearly 40% of jobs globally and 60% in advanced economies. Stanford researchers found no economy-wide displacement but a 19% employment gap for 22-to-25-year-olds in exposed occupations, largely through reduced hiring, while Yale’s Budget Lab has yet to find a clear AI-related labor-market footprint. Gates acknowledged that his warning is a forecast, not a reading of today’s topline employment data. Many of the risks Gates outlines are specific to richer, Western countries. And Gates said virtually all of the fixes will require governments to play a role. He dismissed the idea that philanthropies — his Gates Foundation is the largest in the world — can create solutions. “Government is 20 times bigger than all philanthropy, so no, philanthropy cannot solve the safety-net issue,” Gates said. “I’m by far the biggest philanthropy in the world. And what are we? We’re $10 billion a year.” The private sector, too, is ill-equipped to handle the problem on its own, Gates argued. Model builders are “not policy people,” he said, and have “a little bit of a bias against talking about the potential negatives of their products.” “The response can’t be, ‘Hey industry, you solve this,’” he said. Gates’ Solutions Gates outlined several possible solutions, including government mandates designating certain occupations or services as “human reserved” — work that would remain the province of people even if machines could do it more efficiently. “So what if we declare something human-reserved that we shouldn’t?” he said. “The capitalistic signals are here to serve humans.” Another idea: taxing AI compute tokens and robots. Gates said a usage tax would directly change companies’ incentives to replace workers, unlike a corporate tax that only captures profits — which may be limited in a hypercompetitive market. Labor is already taxed through payroll levies, he noted, while robots can be depreciated, and carry no Social Security tax. “Today, we are very pro-robot in our tax policies, and I’m saying I think that’s a mistake,” he said. Gates cautioned against assuming the companies building the most consequential AI systems will capture most of the wealth they create. Intense competition could commoditize models, he said, much as fiber optics and disk storage transformed the economy without producing a corresponding class of obvious winners. “You can actually have technologies that change the world very, very dramatically, and there’s no profit created,” Gates said. At today’s commodity level, he added, users may pay for execution and inference but little or nothing for a model’s intellectual property — which could allow more of the economic benefit to flow to customers and downstream businesses. Gates brushed aside the idea that his suggestions might draw pushback from the accelerationist voices in the tech industry. He said he has no financial reason to hold back.
